docs.title: Home 👋
docs.text:
mangoo I/O is a lean, opinionated full-stack Java web framework that scales out securely, no assembly required. It builds HTTP applications, everything from server-rendered HTML sites to JSON APIs, on Undertow and follows a classic MVC style: you map URLs to controller methods, return a Response, and optionally render Freemarker templates or send JSON.

Controllers live in a package you configure once, templates follow a predictable path, and sessions, flash, CSRF, and locale are method parameters. Routes are Java code in app.Bootstrap. Configuration is one YAML file. Dependency injection is Google Guice. The application module has to be named app.Module.

If you are new to the project, start with Getting started. It walks through the Maven archetype, the project layout, and the first request. The libraries underneath are Undertow, Guice, Freemarker, Jackson, the MongoDB driver, Caffeine, and Log4j2.

docs.title: How a request flows
docs.text:
At a high level, every HTTP request passes through Undertow, then any filters you have registered, then a controller method you mapped in app.Bootstrap:

  1. Routing. Bootstrap.initializeRoutes() registers URLs. A route points to a controller class and a method name, nothing more indirect than that.
  2. Bindings. The framework injects path parameters, query values, JSON bodies, and objects such as Request, Session, Form, or Authentication directly into the method signature, based on the parameter types and names you declare.
  3. Response. The method returns Response.ok(), Response.redirect(...), or similar. You choose whether to render a template, send JSON, or just return a status.

A minimal example ties these three steps together:

public Response index(Request request, Session session) {
    return Response.ok().render("username", session.get("username"));
}

Templates, cookies, and security headers are handled by the framework once you return the response, so controller code stays focused on what your application actually does rather than on plumbing.

docs.title: What you get out of the box
docs.text:
mangoo I/O ships as mangooio-core, plus mangooio-test and the Maven plugin. Undertow, Freemarker, and Jackson are already wired. You can replace a binding in app.Module, including Datastore, when the default is the wrong one.

Area Built-in support HTTP server Undertow (HTTP and optional HTTPS) Templates Freemarker JSON Jackson Persistence MongoDB (Java sync driver) Cache Caffeine DI Google Guice Logging Log4j2 Scheduling @Run on plain Java methods Real-time Server-Sent Events; local WebSocket routes Security Encrypted cookies, CSRF, CORS, optional TOTP

Custom filters and extra Guice bindings are the normal way to extend this. Most applications stay on the defaults above.

docs.title: Stack and quality
docs.text:
The runtime stack is small and built on libraries that are maintained outside this project:

  • Undertow for non-blocking I/O and low overhead
  • Google Guice for constructor injection and testability
  • Freemarker for server-side HTML
  • MongoDB Java driver for document storage with POJO codecs
  • Caffeine for in-process caching
  • Log4j2 for logging
  • Jackson (with Blackbird) for JSON

Each release is validated against a large SonarQube rule set. The core module is kept intentionally compact: functionality that only matters for tests (mangooio-test) or for tooling (mangooio-maven-plugin) lives in its own artifact instead of bloating what every production app has to ship.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
• Convention over configuration. Controller package, template paths, and translation bundles follow fixed conventions, so you spend less time on boilerplate and more time writing the parts unique to your app.
  • Restart on compile in dev mode. mvn mangooio:run does not compile. It restarts the process after target/classes changes, once the writes have settled (500 ms by default). The JVM start is on top of that. Templates reload without a restart.
  • Programmatic routing. All routes live in Bootstrap.java. There is no separate routes file that can drift out of sync with the code that actually handles the request.
  • Maven archetype. Generates a working app with generated dev and test secrets, sample persistence, and a first test already in place.

docs.title: HTTP and security
docs.text:
• Fluent Response API. Status codes, headers, cookies, redirects, HTML, JSON, and binary bodies all share one builder-style API, so you are not switching mental models depending on what you are returning.
  • Client-side sessions and flash. Session and flash data live in encrypted and signed JWT cookies. Any instance with the same secrets, cookie names, and application.name can serve the next request. There is no sticky session and no shared session store.
  • Form validation. The Form object uses the same validation helpers as regular request handling, with messages sourced from messages.properties so error text stays translatable.
  • CSRF and origin checks. Filters for token validation and allowed Origin headers integrate directly with Freemarker directives, so protecting a form is a template tag, not a manual token dance.
  • Cookie authentication. You verify credentials however you like; the framework issues and validates the auth cookie for you. Optional TOTP is available for two-factor login.

docs.title: Data and background work
docs.text:
• MongoDB datastore. Inject Datastore, map entities with @Collection, and query using the native driver API rather than a framework-specific abstraction on top of it.
  • Built-in cache. A Caffeine cache in the process. Login lockouts are kept in MongoDB when persistence is on, so instances share them. Token revocation is separate and off until authentication.blacklist is true.
  • @Run scheduler. Fixed-delay (Every 5m) or cron-style jobs on ordinary classes, discovered automatically through a classpath scan at startup.
  • EventBus. publish returns immediately. Subscribers for that payload then run one after another on a virtual thread, on the instance that published. Cross-instance delivery is the MessageBroker, used by SSE.
  • Asynchronous email. Jakarta Mail integration where Mail.send() does not block the request thread, so sending a confirmation email never adds latency to the response the user is waiting on.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
• Admin dashboard. An optional /@admin UI for cache stats, the scheduler, and a few security helpers. In prod the cookie requires HTTPS.
  • Health and shutdown. /@health/live and /@health/ready are always on. Shutdown starts with readiness going to 503 and waits up to application.shutdown.timeout (20 seconds).
  • Metrics and tracing. Dashboard metrics are off until metrics.enable. OpenTelemetry export is off until otlp.enable.
  • Fat-JAR deployment. The shade plugin produces a single runnable JAR. Operating covers supervisord, Docker, probes, cookies, and the request-size limits.

docs.title: Documentation map
docs.text:
The sidebar groups topics by concern. A typical learning path looks like this:

  1. Getting started: install Java 25 and Maven, generate a project, run it locally.
  2. Configuration and Secrets: config.yaml, modes, environment variables, secret files, HTTPS.
  3. Bootstrap and Routing: lifecycle hooks and URL mapping.
  4. Controllers and Templating: request handling, parameters, Freemarker.
  5. Working with JSON: APIs and POJO binding.
  6. Authentication, Sessions, CSRF: security building blocks.
  7. Persistence: MongoDB entities and queries.
  8. Testing and Operating: tests against a running app and production deployment.

Reference pages cover filters, forms, flash, caching, emails, scheduler, SSE, async, i18n, utils, logging, administration, and observability.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text: When you move between major or minor versions, read the changelog and migrations first. Breaking changes, for example the removal of the vault in 11.0, or from Paseto to JWT in the 10.x line, are documented there with pointers to whichever guide reflects the current behavior.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:
• Source and issues: github.com/svenkubiak/mangooio
  • Maven coordinates: io.mangoo:mangooio-core (see Maven Central for the latest version)

docs.title: Administration
docs.text:
The admin dashboard is a built-in UI for operators. It shows uptime, the Java version, heap, open connections, active features, event queues, routes, cache statistics, scheduler jobs, a few security helpers, and request metrics when those are enabled. Clearing a cache and resetting metrics go through the MessageBroker when persistence is on, so they run on every instance. Without persistence they run on the instance that served the page. The instance list is every instance's last heartbeat. The blocks under that list are the instance that served the page. The dashboard is disabled by default. It exposes internal state, so turn it on only where the network is already closed off.

Access uses a login form and JWT cookie rather than HTTP Basic. An optional TOTP second factor is configured with application.admin.secret. In production, protect admin routes with network policy as well as strong credentials kept outside the artifact (see Secrets), since the login form alone is not a substitute for keeping the dashboard off the public internet.

Enable and configure:

application:
  admin:
    enable: true
    username: admin
    password: env{}
    locale: en_EN

application.admin.password stores the Argon2id hash, not the cleartext. From the application project:

mvn -q mangooio:hash

The goal reads src/main/resources/config.yaml and hashes with authentication.hashing.memory, authentication.hashing.iterations and authentication.hashing.parallelism. It merges default with the dev environment. -Dapplication.mode=prod (or test) uses that environment instead; any other value uses prod. -Dapplication.config=/path/to/config.yaml reads another file. The password is prompted twice and is not echoed, so run the goal from a terminal. The prompts and the PHC string are indented under a short heading. -q hides the Maven log around that block. The application does not have to be running, and no login is required.

Pass that string as application.admin.password, for example in APPLICATION_ADMIN_PASSWORD. The salt is part of the hash, and the goal picks a random one with CommonUtils.uuidV4. There is no separate salt setting. The goal calls CommonUtils.hashArgon2 with the three parameters from the config file. The two-argument form still needs a started application, because it uses that application's hasher. Passing application.secret as the salt embeds that secret in the stored hash.

Open:

http://<host>:<port>/@admin

You sign in with a form at /@admin/login. A JWT cookie is issued for later requests. This is not HTTP Basic authentication.

The cookie name is mangooio-admin. In prod it is __Host-mangooio-admin, which browsers accept only on HTTPS, with Secure and Path=/. It is HttpOnly and SameSite=Strict. Secure is set only in prod mode, so a prod deployment on plain HTTP will not keep the operator signed in. The full session lasts 1800 seconds. After the password and before TOTP, the TTL is 120 seconds and the cookie is single-use (OneTimeStore key admin-pre-auth: plus the JWT id). Signing and encryption use application.secret for both the HMAC key and the AES secret. The issuer is application.name. The audience is the cookie name.

Routes registered when application.admin.enable is true: GET /@admin, /@admin/cache, /@admin/login, /@admin/twofactor, /@admin/scheduler, /@admin/routes, /@admin/security, /@admin/logout, and POST /@admin/authenticate, /@admin/verify, /@admin/cache/clear, /@admin/metrics/reset. POST mutations use CsrfFilter. /@admin/assets/ is a public classpath resource handler. /@admin/stream sits outside AdminFilter and returns 401 with no body when the cookie is missing, invalid, or still the pre-auth cookie. The page script then shows the login form. A hidden tab closes the EventSource.

Clearing the application cache keeps the MANGOOIO-WARNINGS entry. There is no unlock route for a locked admin login. The documents are _id admin:pwd and admin:2fa in mangooio_attempts. A password that is not a PHC hash is rejected and still consumes an attempt. MangooHashingException releases the attempt.

docs.title: MFA
docs.text:
Set application.admin.secret to a TOTP secret and a second factor kicks in. After the password, /@admin/twofactor asks for a 6-digit code (SHA-512, 30-second period, no adjacent step). Each code and each pre-authentication cookie is accepted once. The lock is not authentication.lock. It is fixed at 10 attempts and 60 minutes, on the keys admin:pwd and admin:2fa, shared across instances when persistence is enabled. The "Login lock" row on the dashboard is the user setting, not this one. A bad password and a lock both send you back to the login form.

GET /@admin/security draws a new TOTP secret on every load while application.admin.secret is unset. That secret is not saved. The QR code is useless until you put the value in config and restart. Generate a secret you intend to keep with TotpUtils, as in Authentication.

docs.title: Several instances
docs.text:
The dashboard starts with the list of instances: id, version, last heartbeat, heap, open connections, and the requests, errors, average time, and failed events of the last five minutes. Every instance reports every ten seconds while the dashboard is enabled, including once at start. With persistence the reports are mangooio_instances. Without persistence only this process is known. An instance that stopped removes itself. One that crashed is marked after 30 seconds without a heartbeat and disappears after a minute. getInstances drops a document whose expireAt is in the past, so the MongoDB TTL monitor is not required for that. If the registry read fails, the page still shows the instance that served it. A rolling deploy shows up as instances with different versions.

Requests, errors, and average time come from Metrics and stay at zero unless metrics.enable is true. Errors are status codes of 500 and above. Times are milliseconds. At most 10 failed routes are listed. Past 1000 distinct route templates, the rest are bucketed as Other routes.

Clearing a cache and resetting the metrics are sent through the MessageBroker and run on every instance. Everything below the list of instances, as well as the pages for routes, scheduler and cache, shows the instance that served the page; its id is marked in the list and shown in the footer.

docs.title: Live updates
docs.text: While the dashboard is open, it connects to /@admin/stream and replaces the instance list, this instance, and the event queues every five seconds. Requests, status codes, routes, and failures are included only when metrics.enable is true. A badge next to the title shows the open stream. The stream requires a valid admin cookie and closes when the cookie expires. The page then shows the login form. A background tab closes the stream and opens it again when the tab is visible. The connection stays on one instance. After that instance restarts, the page connects to whichever instance answers next.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Request counts and timings are off by default, so enable them explicitly:

metrics:
  enable: true

Once enabled, they appear on the dashboard itself: requests, error rate and processing times of the last five minutes with the values since the start below, the responses grouped by status code since the start, the routes with the most client and server errors, and the last 50 server errors with time, route and status. Both show the route template, e.g. GET /user/{id}, never the requested path of a matched route, and no exceptions. A request without a route is shown with its path and without the query string. The exceptions are in the log. They are collected per instance, and the dashboard footer names the instance that served the page. For load balancer probes use /@health/live and /@health/ready, see Operating.

See Observability for OpenTelemetry.

docs.title: Async
docs.text:
The EventBus publishes payloads to Subscriber implementations. publish returns immediately. Delivery of one event runs on a single virtual thread, and the subscribers for that payload are called one after another. A slow subscriber delays the next subscriber of the same event. It does not block the publisher, and it does not run on an Undertow thread.

Subscribers are discovered at startup. The queue name is payload.getClass().getName(). A subclass does not reach a subscriber registered for a parent type. A raw Subscriber or Subscriber<Object> is skipped and logged. There is no unregister. Register another class when you need a second handler for the same payload.

docs.title: Subscribers
docs.text:
Implement io.mangoo.async.Subscriber<T>, and mangoo I/O registers every implementation it finds on startup. The payload type is taken from the type argument T, so declare it explicitly; a raw Subscriber is not registered and logged as a warning. The queue name is the binary name of the payload type, so a Subscriber<String> registers under java.lang.String and a subscriber for a nested record Events.OrderPlaced under com.example.Events$OrderPlaced.

package subscribers;

import io.mangoo.async.Subscriber;

public class AuditSubscriber implements Subscriber<String> {
    @Override
    public void receive(String payload) {
        // handle payload
    }
}

Subscribers are created through Guice, so you can inject dependencies. Every subscriber of a payload is called independently, an exception thrown by one subscriber is logged and does not prevent the others from receiving the payload.

docs.title: Publishing
docs.text:
@Inject
private EventBus eventBus;

public void notify(String message) {
    eventBus.publish(message);
}

publish looks up subscribers for payload.getClass().getName(). You can also call eventBus.register("java.lang.String", AuditSubscriber.class). Classpath scanning already does that for any Subscriber it finds. getHandledEvents(), getFailedEvents(), getSubscribers(), and getNumberOfSubscribers() are what the admin dashboard reads.

EventBus stays on the publishing JVM. Cross-instance messages go through io.mangoo.interfaces.MessageBroker:

void publish(String topic, String message);
void subscribe(String topic, Consumer<String> consumer);

With persistence that is the capped collection mangooio_messages. Without it, subscribers on this JVM only. A message published while the tail is disconnected is not replayed. SSE and the admin cache-clear action use this broker. See Operating.

Use a dedicated payload class if you need separate queues:

public record OrderPlaced(String id) {}

public class OrderSubscriber implements Subscriber<OrderPlaced> {
    @Override
    public void receive(OrderPlaced payload) { }
}

eventBus.publish(new OrderPlaced("42"));

docs.title: Authentication 🔑
docs.text:
mangoo I/O provides cookie-based authentication, not a full user-management system. You remain responsible for storing users, validating passwords, and deciding who may log in; the framework's job starts once you have already decided "yes, this person may in." After a successful check, you call authentication.login(subject) and the framework sets a signed, encrypted JWT cookie on the response.

That design fits applications that already have a user table (or an external identity source) and want session-like behavior without server-side session storage for auth state. Because the cookie itself carries everything needed to verify it, it works in a share-nothing setup: any node behind a load balancer can validate it using the same configured keys, with no shared session store, no sticky sessions, and no "which server did this user log in on" problem to solve.

Optional pieces build on the same model:

  • Remember me. Longer cookie lifetime via rememberMe(), for the "keep me logged in" checkbox users expect.
  • Two-factor. Flag the cookie until TOTP is verified, using TotpUtils and isValidSecondFactor, so a stolen password alone is not enough to authenticate.
  • Route protection. withAuthentication() on routes or controllers, so protecting a page is a one-line addition in Bootstrap.java rather than a check repeated in every method.
  • API keys. ApiKeyFilter for machine clients using the Authorization header, since a script calling your API has no browser to hold a cookie for it.

Inject Authentication into a controller method:

public Response login(Authentication authentication) {
    return Response.ok().render();
}

docs.title: Password hashing
docs.text:
Hash passwords with Argon2id via CommonUtils. Argon2id was chosen because it is memory-hard: unlike older algorithms such as bcrypt or SHA-based hashes, it is deliberately expensive to parallelize on GPUs, which is exactly the kind of attack password hashes need to resist once a database leaks.

String hash = CommonUtils.hashArgon2("password", "salt");

Store the hash (and the salt) with your user record; never store the plain password anywhere, not even temporarily in a log line.

The returned value is a PHC string that carries the parameters and the salt it was created with:

$argon2id$v=19$m=32768,t=3,p=1$<salt-b64>$<hash-b64>

Because the parameters travel with the hash, matchArgon2 verifies with the parameters of the stored hash and never with the current configuration. Changing authentication.hashing.memory, authentication.hashing.iterations or authentication.hashing.parallelism therefore does not lock anybody out.

The salt you pass to matchArgon2 still has to be the one the hash was created with. The embedded salt is not used as a fallback: if the two differ, the verification fails. A hash whose embedded salt someone swapped out is rejected rather than verified against the attacker's salt.

Note

The salt ends up in the stored string, as the PHC format prescribes. If you pass a secret as the salt — hashArgon2(cleartext) uses application.secret — it is no longer secret once the hash is stored. Use a per-user random salt and keep a pepper out of the hash.

Because Argon2id is memory-hard, every call holds authentication.hashing.memory KiB of heap (32 MB by default) for as long as it runs. The framework limits how many of these computations may run at the same time, so that a burst of concurrent logins cannot exhaust the heap. A call that finds every slot taken waits up to authentication.hashing.timeout milliseconds and is then rejected with a MangooHashingException. See Argon2 hashing for the configuration and for what happens on the individual call sites.

docs.title: Rehashing
docs.text:
A stored value that is not in PHC format was created by a mangoo I/O version before 10.13.0. It is verified with the parameters that version used (m=80000,t=6,p=2) and the salt you pass in, so an upgrade does not lock out existing users.

CommonUtils.needsRehash tells you whether a stored hash should be replaced — true for a legacy hash and for a PHC hash whose parameters differ from the current configuration:

if (authentication.isValidLogin(identifier, password, salt, hash)) {
    if (CommonUtils.needsRehash(hash)) {
        user.setPassword(CommonUtils.hashArgon2(password, salt));
        datastore.save(user);
    }
    authentication.login(identifier);
}

Warning

Only evaluate needsRehash after a successful verification. Recomputing a hash needs the clear text, and only a successful login proves that the clear text is the right one.

docs.title: Login
docs.text:
if (authentication.isValidLogin("subject", "password", "salt", "hash")) {
    authentication.login("subject");
}

isValidLogin also applies lockout: after authentication.lock failed attempts (default 10), the identifier is locked for authentication.lock.duration minutes (default 60). This happens automatically so that a brute-force attempt against one account gets throttled without you having to implement rate limiting by hand. A successful login clears the budget.

If no hashing slot becomes available within authentication.hashing.timeout, isValidLogin fails closed and returns false. The failed attempt budget stays untouched in that case, an overload situation must not lock a user out.

The lockout is an absolute point in time, set once when the budget is used up. Further failed attempts during the lockout are rejected without extending it, so an attacker cannot keep the rightful owner of an account locked out indefinitely by simply continuing to guess.

The same budget applies to the second factor, see Two-factor authentication. Both steps are counted separately per identifier, so a failed password attempt never consumes the budget of the second factor and vice versa.

With persistence enabled the budget is kept in MongoDB (mangooio_attempts), so several instances behind a load balancer share one budget per identifier and a restart does not reset it. The lock time is computed by the database, clock differences between the instances do not shift it. If MongoDB is unavailable, the attempt is refused and the identifier counts as locked. Without persistence the budget is kept in memory per process. Bind your own io.mangoo.interfaces.AttemptStore in app.Module to keep it elsewhere. See Framework collections for all collections the framework creates.

rememberMe() and twoFactorAuthentication(boolean) only set fields. The cookie is written when login() or update() has marked it for this response. Call them in the same request, before the method returns:

authentication.login(username);
authentication.rememberMe();

twoFactorAuthentication(true) is the same kind of flag. Set it in that same request, before the method returns. On a later request, either call alone does not rewrite a cookie that is already valid. Call update() as well.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
authentication.getSubject();   // logged-in subject, or null
authentication.isValid();      // authentication is complete, use this for authorization
authentication.hasSubject();   // a subject is present, second factor may still be pending
authentication.logout();       // expire the cookie
authentication.invalidate();   // expire the cookie
authentication.update();       // refresh the cookie on this response
authentication.rememberMe(true);
authentication.twoFactorAuthentication(true);
authentication.userHasLock("subject");              // password step
authentication.userHasSecondFactorLock("subject");  // second factor step
authentication.isValidSecondFactor("subject", secret, totp);

isValid() and hasSubject() are not interchangeable. hasSubject() is the raw check whether a subject is set, which is already the case right after the password step, because that is when the authentication cookie is issued. isValid() additionally requires that no second factor is outstanding, and it is the one to base an authorization decision on. Use hasSubject() only where the incomplete state is exactly the state you are working on, which in practice is the page that asks for the TOTP.

This matters because an Authentication object is bound on every request, not only on routes bound with withAuthentication(). A filter or controller method on an unprotected route that derives access from getSubject() alone lets a visitor in who knows the password but not the second factor.

userHasLock() and userHasSecondFactorLock() are queries, not a step you have to perform. isValidLogin() and isValidSecondFactor() check the lock before doing any work and count the failed attempt afterwards, both on their own. Query the lock only where you want to show "this account is locked" instead of the same "login failed" that a wrong password produces.

logout() and invalidate() behave identically: both expire the authentication cookie with the current response and, with authentication.blacklist, revoke its token.

docs.title: Protecting routes
docs.text:
Bind.controller(AccountController.class).withRoutes(
    On.get().to("/account").respondeWith("index").withAuthentication()
);

You can also call withAuthentication() on the controller binder so every route on it requires a cookie, see Routing. Missing authentication redirects to authentication.redirect.login (the archetype sets /login), or returns HTTP 403 if that key is unset. When two-factor is still pending, the user is sent to authentication.redirect.mfa, or to the login redirect if mfa is not set. Set authentication.origin to append the request URI. The separator is ? when the redirect has no query string and & when it already has one. The value is URL-encoded and always starts with one slash, which encoding turns into %2F, so it cannot arrive as //evil.com.

That last point still leaves the final decision to you: origin is a value a visitor chose, and it is only guaranteed to be a path on your own host, not a path that visitor is allowed to reach. Before redirecting to it after a successful login, check it against the routes your application actually serves rather than passing it straight to a redirect.

Route protection covers controller routes only. SSE and WebSocket routes are registered straight on Undertow's path handler and never reach the authentication check, so withAuthentication() does not exist on them and no cookie is verified when a client connects. See Routing for what that means in practice.

Cookie names, SameSite, Secure, signing keys, and lifetimes are described in Configuration. Set authentication.cookie.key and authentication.cookie.secret with env{}, arg{} or file{} rather than writing them out in config.yaml; in prod mode literal values fail the startup. See Secrets.

docs.title: Two-factor authentication
docs.text:
Generate a secret and verify TOTP codes with TotpUtils (SHA-512, 6 digits, 30-second period, the same parameters most authenticator apps expect out of the box):

String secret = TotpUtils.createSecret();
String qr = TotpUtils.getQRCode("user@example.com", "My App", secret);
String url = TotpUtils.getOtpAuthURL("user@example.com", "My App", secret);

if (authentication.isValidSecondFactor(subject, secret, totpFromUser)) {
    authentication.twoFactorAuthentication(false);
    authentication.update();
}

A typical flow: after the password check succeeds, call login(subject) with twoFactorAuthentication(true) set, redirect to your TOTP entry page, and only clear the flag once isValidSecondFactor confirms the code the user typed in actually matches their secret. Call update() afterwards so the cleared flag reaches the cookie on that same response. See Complete login flow for both steps written out.

While the flag is set, isValid() returns false, so the TOTP entry page itself has to use hasSubject() to find the subject the code is being checked for.

Pass the identifier as the first argument. A TOTP has six digits and is verified without a tolerance window, so exactly one of a million codes is valid per 30-second window — that is only a second factor as long as something limits how often it may be guessed. With the identifier, the same authentication.lock budget as for the password step applies, counted under its own key, and a successful check clears it. An upstream reverse proxy only counts requests per source address and does not bound the total number of guesses; a budget per identity does.

Each code is accepted once per identifier: the used 30-second step is stored in the OneTimeStore (MongoDB with persistence, shared by all instances), so a code that was observed on its way cannot be replayed within its window; the collection is mangooio_claims, see Framework collections. TotpUtils.verifyTotp(identifier, secret, totp) does the same outside of Authentication; TotpUtils.verifyTotp(secret, totp) without an identifier accepts a valid code any number of times.

docs.title: Complete login flow
docs.text: The flows below show every call to Authentication a controller needs — and nothing else. In particular there is no lock handling in them: isValidLogin and isValidSecondFactor check the lock before they do any work and count the failed attempt afterwards, both on their own. Querying the lock is a separate, optional step, see Telling a lock apart.

docs.title: Without two-factor
docs.text:
public Response doLogin(Form form, Authentication authentication, Flash flash) {
    String username = form.get("username");
    User user = userService.findByUsername(username);

    if (user == null || !authentication.isValidLogin(username, form.get("password"), user.getSalt(), user.getPassword())) {
        flash.setError("Login failed");
        return Response.redirect("/login");
    }

    authentication.login(username);
    if (form.getBoolean("remember").orElse(false)) {
        authentication.rememberMe();
    }

    return Response.redirect("/dashboard");
}

No update() here: login() writes a fresh cookie on its own, even if the browser still sends a stale one.

docs.title: With two-factor
docs.text:
The password step is the same up to the last two calls:

    authentication.login(username);
    authentication.twoFactorAuthentication(true);

    return Response.redirect("/twofactor");

From here on isValid() is false and hasSubject() is true. The cookie is written regardless and carries the flag, which is what keeps the second step stateless.

The page that asks for the code must not be bound with withAuthentication(). That route protection redirects to authentication.redirect.mfa exactly while the flag is set, so the TOTP page would redirect to itself:

public Response twofactor(Authentication authentication) {
    if (!authentication.hasSubject()) {
        return Response.redirect("/login");
    }

    return Response.ok().render();
}

public Response doTwofactor(Form form, Authentication authentication, Flash flash) {
    if (!authentication.hasSubject()) {
        return Response.redirect("/login");
    }

    String subject = authentication.getSubject();
    User user = userService.findByUsername(subject);

    if (!authentication.isValidSecondFactor(subject, user.getTotpSecret(), form.get("totp"))) {
        flash.setError("Invalid code");
        return Response.redirect("/twofactor");
    }

    authentication.twoFactorAuthentication(false);
    authentication.update();

    return Response.redirect("/dashboard");
}

update() is mandatory in this step. The authentication cookie already exists at this point and is only rewritten when it is missing or when update() asked for it — without it the cookie keeps twoFactor=true and the next request sends the user back to /twofactor.

docs.title: Logout
docs.text:
public Response doLogout(Authentication authentication) {
    authentication.logout();
    return Response.redirect("/");
}

docs.title: Telling a lock apart
docs.text:
Nothing above has to change for the lockout to work. A locked identifier makes isValidLogin return false without checking the password, which is the same false a wrong password produces — so the user is told "login failed" while the account is in fact locked.

Add a lock query only if you want a different message for that case:

    if (authentication.userHasLock(username)) {
        flash.setError("Account is temporarily locked, try again later");
        return Response.redirect("/login");
    }

userHasSecondFactorLock(subject) does the same for the TOTP step. Both are read-only: they neither consume an attempt nor set a lock, so an extra query costs nothing but also protects nothing on its own.

Be aware that this is a trade-off, not a free improvement. A message that distinguishes "locked" from "wrong password" confirms to whoever triggered the lock that the identifier exists. On a login form that already reveals existing accounts elsewhere, for example on registration or password reset, that changes nothing; on one that deliberately does not, keep the single generic message.

docs.title: What the controller does not see
docs.text:
A hashing overload is reported to isValidLogin as false, indistinguishable from a wrong password. That is deliberate, see Argon2 hashing; the failed attempt budget stays untouched, so the situation cannot lock anyone out. If you need to tell the two apart, call CommonUtils.matchArgon2 yourself and catch MangooHashingException — at the price of losing the built-in lock handling.

Your own hashing outside the login path, on registration or a password change, needs no try/catch. The unchecked MangooHashingException travels to the ExceptionHandler and becomes a 503. Catching it and returning false would turn an overload into a silent "wrong password".

docs.title: API keys
docs.text:
For machine clients that have no browser and therefore nowhere to keep a cookie, use ApiKeyFilter instead:

application:
  api:
    key: env{}

@FilterWith(ApiKeyFilter.class)
public Response export() {
    return Response.ok().bodyJson(data);
}

The filter reads Authorization, strips the literal substring Bearer (case-sensitive), and compares the remainder to application.api.key. Authorization: Bearer <key> and Authorization: <key> both match. A missing or wrong key is HTTP 401 with an empty body. If the key is set, startup requires at least 64 bytes.

This is one shared key, not a credential per client. Rotate it if it leaks. There is no per-caller revocation.

docs.title: Blacklist
docs.text:
Set authentication.blacklist to true to revoke authentication cookies before their natural expiry. Revocations are handled by an io.mangoo.interfaces.TokenBlacklist, which you can inject like any other component.

  • Logout. authentication.logout() and authentication.invalidate() revoke the token of the current cookie automatically. A copy of that cookie, for example a stolen one, is rejected from then on until the token would have expired anyway.
  • All tokens of an account. revokeSubject(subject) revokes every token of a subject that was issued before now, for example right after a user changed their password or an account was compromised. Tokens issued afterwards, such as a new login in the same request, stay valid, so the user is not locked out.
@Inject
private TokenBlacklist tokenBlacklist;

public Response changePassword(Authentication authentication) {
    // ... update the password
    tokenBlacklist.revokeSubject(authentication.getSubject());
    authentication.login(authentication.getSubject());
    return Response.redirect("/");
}

Every revocation is kept exactly as long as the revoked token could still be accepted, that is until its expiry or, for a subject, for the longest token lifetime (authentication.cookie.remember.expires or authentication.cookie.token.expires), plus the 30 second clock tolerance of the JWT validation.

With persistence enabled, revocations are kept in MongoDB (mangooio_revocations): they survive a restart and apply to every instance behind a load balancer. Each authenticated request costs one lookup on the primary key; if MongoDB is unavailable, the cookie counts as revoked. Without persistence, revocations are kept in memory, only apply to the instance that received them and are lost on a restart.

To keep revocations elsewhere, bind your own implementation in your Module. It replaces the one of the framework:

public class Module extends AbstractModule {
    @Override
    protected void configure() {
        bind(TokenBlacklist.class).to(RedisTokenBlacklist.class);
    }
}

To invalidate every issued authentication cookie at once, independent of the blacklist, rotate authentication.cookie.secret.

docs.title: Bootstrap 🔧
docs.text:
The bootstrap class is the main extension point for application wiring: it is where routes get registered and where you hook into startup and shutdown. It implements MangooBootstrap and is bound in app.Module. Most projects use a class named Bootstrap in the app package, since that is what the archetype generates, but nothing forces that name on you (see Getting started for the generated version).

You use it for three kinds of work:

  1. Routes. initializeRoutes() registers every URL before the server starts accepting traffic, so by the time the first request can possibly arrive, the whole route table already exists.
  2. Startup and shutdown. Hooks (all four must be implemented, but may stay empty) run after configuration is loaded, after connectors are listening, and when the JVM shuts down, giving you three distinct moments to plug into instead of one big "app started" event.
  3. Cross-cutting setup. For example, global security headers via Server.header(...) at the start of initializeRoutes(). They are copied onto controller responses, the 404 page, error pages, and authentication redirects. They are not applied to SSE, WebSocket handshakes, static files, or the early 400 for a bad query string. A blank value is not sent, which is why the built-in Content-Security-Policy stays absent until you set one.

Because Bootstrap is a normal Guice-managed type, you can inject services (a Datastore, a cache, your own service class) and use them in applicationStarted() to seed data or warm caches, exactly the way the archetype's sample app seeds a few Person records.

package app;

import io.mangoo.interfaces.MangooBootstrap;

public class Bootstrap implements MangooBootstrap {

    @Override
    public void initializeRoutes() {
        // Bind.controller(...).withRoutes(...)
    }

    @Override
    public void applicationInitialized() {
        // Config is loaded and the Guice injector exists,
        // but no routes are registered and no connector is listening yet
    }

    @Override
    public void applicationStarted() {
        // HTTP/HTTPS listeners are up and accepting requests;
        // a good place to seed data or warm a cache
    }

    @Override
    public void applicationStopped() {
        // JVM shutdown signal received;
        // close whatever you opened yourself (a connection pool, a file handle)
    }
}

The four methods run in this order: applicationInitialized(), initializeRoutes(), applicationStarted(), applicationStopped(). applicationInitialized() runs before config validation and before any route exists. applicationStarted() runs after the connectors are listening, and too late to change the route table. applicationStopped() runs after Undertow has stopped, while the MongoDB clients are still open. The full sequence, including the classpath scan that overlaps initializeRoutes(), is in Getting started.

The bootstrap class name is arbitrary. It has to implement MangooBootstrap and be bound in app.Module. The module class itself is not arbitrary: the framework loads app.Module by name.

package app;

import com.google.inject.AbstractModule;
import io.mangoo.interfaces.MangooBootstrap;

public class Module extends AbstractModule {
    @Override
    protected void configure() {
        bind(MangooBootstrap.class).to(Bootstrap.class);
    }
}

That single bind(...) line is how mangoo I/O locates your application at startup, so if you ever rename your bootstrap class, this is the one place you have to remember to update. Put extra Guice bindings in the same configure() method rather than scattering them elsewhere. See Dependency injection and Routing.

initializeRoutes() is also a convenient place for global response headers, since it runs exactly once, before any request handling starts:

Server.header(Header.CONTENT_SECURITY_POLICY, "default-src 'self'");
Server.header(Header.X_FRAME_OPTIONS, "DENY");

Use this for headers you want on ordinary pages. SSE, static files, and WebSocket handshakes do not pick them up. See Operating for the headers the framework already sends.

docs.title: Caching
docs.text:
Repeated expensive lookups, such as database reads, external API calls, or computed aggregates, benefit from an in-process cache. mangoo I/O wraps Caffeine and exposes an injectable Cache for the default application cache, plus named caches for when you need separate eviction policies or key spaces.

Entries expire after write (30 days by default). You can attach a fallback function so a get on a missing key loads and stores it automatically instead of returning null. Counter helpers cover rate limiting or metrics-style increments without needing a separate store.

Inject io.mangoo.cache.Cache for the application cache:

@Inject
private Cache cache;

cache.put("foo", "bar");
String value = cache.get("foo");
cache.remove("foo");
cache.clear();

Entries in the application cache expire 30 days after write (not after last access), and the cache holds at most 50 000 keys.

docs.title: TTL and fallback
docs.text:
cache.put("foo", "bar", 10, ChronoUnit.MINUTES);
cache.put("foo", "bar", LocalDateTime.now().plusHours(1));

String value = cache.get("foo", key -> loadFromDatabase(key));
String timed = cache.get("foo", 5, ChronoUnit.MINUTES, key -> loadFromDatabase(key));

The fallback is a Function<String, Object>. A non-null result is stored, so the next get skips the function. A null result is not stored.

get(key) and get(key, amount, unit, fallback) honour a per-entry expiry from put(key, value, amount, unit). get(key, fallback) does not. It reads Caffeine directly and can return a value past that timestamp, until the cache-wide 30-day expiry. Use the timed overload when the fallback must respect the short TTL. Putting null removes a cached value.

cache.putAll(Map.of("a", 1, "b", 2));
Map<String, Object> batch = cache.getAll("a", "b");

docs.title: Counters
docs.text:
long logins = cache.increment("logins");   // new value, a missing counter starts at 0
cache.decrement("logins");
cache.getCounter("logins");                // 0 if the counter does not exist
cache.resetCounter("logins");

increment and decrement are atomic. A missing counter starts from the delta, so the first increment stores 1 and the first decrement stores -1. A key that holds something other than a Long throws IllegalStateException. A counter expires with the cache, or earlier if it was put with an expiry.

docs.title: Named caches
docs.text:
The application cache (CacheName.APPLICATION) is the default Cache injection; it evicts 30 days after write and holds 50 000 keys. Failed login attempts, one-time claims and token revocations are not kept in a cache but in the AttemptStore, OneTimeStore and TokenBlacklist, which are shared through MongoDB when persistence is enabled, see Operating.

The cache is local to each instance. Bind your own Cache in app.Module when entries have to be shared. getCache(name) returns null for a name that was never added. addCache refuses the application cache name, ignoring case. CacheImpl.getStats() exists for the dashboard. The Cache interface does not expose it.

@Inject
public MyService(CacheProvider cacheProvider) {
    Cache cache = cacheProvider.getCache(CacheName.APPLICATION);
}

Register extra caches with cacheProvider.addCache(name, cache); caches of type CacheImpl show up on the admin dashboard alongside the application cache.

docs.title: Version 11.0.0
docs.text:
Released at 09.11.2026

  • Behaviour change smtp.protocol smtptls requires STARTTLS, smtp is cleartext and refused in prod, and an SMTP connection or read that exceeds smtp.connection.timeout or smtp.read.timeout (10 seconds and 30 seconds by default) is aborted and logged (svenkubiak)
  • Behaviour change Graceful shutdown: readiness goes down, SSE and WebSocket connections are closed, open requests and running @Run tasks get application.shutdown.timeout, then applicationStopped() is called (svenkubiak)
  • Behaviour change A binding in app.Module replaces the core binding of the same type instead of failing (svenkubiak)
  • Behaviour change Removed the vault and vault{}, secrets come from env{}, arg{} or file{} (svenkubiak)
  • Behaviour change An env{}, arg{} or file{} without value and fallback fails the startup (svenkubiak)
  • Behaviour change Framework secrets must not be literal in the config.yaml of the classpath in prod mode (svenkubiak)
  • Behaviour change The HTTPS connector reads its certificate from connector.https.keystore, no self-signed certificate is generated (svenkubiak)
  • Behaviour change The HTTPS connector accepts TLS 1.3 only, TLS 1.2 is refused (svenkubiak)
  • Behaviour change Failed login budgets, admin pre-authentication and token revocations are kept in MongoDB and shared by all instances when persistence is enabled; MongoDB 4.2 is required (svenkubiak)
  • Behaviour change isValidSecondFactor and the admin login accept each TOTP code once (svenkubiak)
  • Behaviour change Removed AuthenticationLock and CacheName.AUTH (svenkubiak)
  • Behaviour change Cache counters are atomic and return long: increment, decrement, getCounter, resetCounter replace getAndIncrementCounter and getAndDecrementCounter (svenkubiak)
  • Behaviour change OpenTelemetry uses application.name as service.name instead of io.mangoo (svenkubiak)
  • Behaviour change The session cookie ends with the browser session unless session.cookie.expires is true (svenkubiak)
  • Behaviour change Removed the unused application.controller (svenkubiak)
  • Removed all deprecated methods (svenkubiak)
  • Removed asset minification (svenkubiak)
  • Migrated from Jackson 2 to Jackson 3 (svenkubiak)
  • Grouped the features of the admin dashboard into security, persistence, connectivity and operations with their values, risky settings are marked in prod mode (svenkubiak)
  • Changed Admin-Password handling (svenkubiak)
  • Redesigned the admin dashboard with Blades CSS instead of Bulma, with dark mode and mobile layout (svenkubiak)
  • Added support for MongoDB connection strings - replica sets, sharded clusters, SRV (svenkubiak)
  • Added responses by status code, Java version and heap, cache clearing and metrics reset to the admin dashboard; with persistence cache clearing and metrics reset run on all instances (svenkubiak)
  • Added a routes page, open connections, event queues, failed events and active features to the admin dashboard (svenkubiak)
  • Added application.name to the brand and page title of the admin dashboard (svenkubiak)
  • Added mvn mangooio:hash to print an Argon2id hash for application.admin.password from the project's config.yaml without starting the application (svenkubiak)
  • Added CommonUtils.hashArgon2(cleartext, salt, settings) to hash with explicit Argon2 settings without a started application (svenkubiak)
  • Added EventBus.getFailedEvents, EventBus.getSubscribers, Application.getServerSentEventConnections and Application.getWebSocketConnections (svenkubiak)
  • Added a list of all instances with heartbeat, version and the requests and errors of the last five minutes to the admin dashboard, shared through mangooio_instances with persistence (svenkubiak)
  • Added live updates of the admin dashboard every five seconds through the server sent event stream /@admin/stream, which requires the admin cookie (svenkubiak)
  • Added the failed requests per route and the last 50 server errors to the admin dashboard (svenkubiak)
  • Added the request metrics of the last five minutes with Metrics.getWindow (svenkubiak)
  • Added health endpoints /@health/live and /@health/ready (svenkubiak)
  • Added connector.proxy to take client address and scheme from X-Forwarded-* headers (svenkubiak)
  • Added an instance id to the startup log, the admin dashboard and the OpenTelemetry resource (svenkubiak)
  • Added a startup warning for embedded MongoDB in prod mode (svenkubiak)
  • Added file{} to read secrets from mounted files in /run/secrets (svenkubiak)
  • Added generated dev and test secrets to the archetype (svenkubiak)
  • Added AttemptStore, OneTimeStore and TotpUtils.verifyTotp(identifier, secret, totp) (svenkubiak)
  • Added MessageBroker, server sent events reach the clients of every instance when persistence is enabled (svenkubiak)
  • Added the OpenTelemetry metric http.server.request.duration when otlp.enable is true (svenkubiak)
  • Added the instance id as system property mangooio.instance.id for log patterns (svenkubiak)
  • Added env{?}, arg{?} and file{?} for optional values, which leave the key unset if the source is empty (svenkubiak)
  • Added persistence.mongo.schema: validate to check collections and indexes at startup instead of creating them (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed a revoked authentication cookie being accepted again within the JWT clock skew after its expiry (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed MongoDB clients not being closed and embedded MongoDB being stopped before Undertow on shutdown (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed the admin login with a second factor failing when the two steps reached different instances (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed a hashing overload failing the admin login with an error instead of refusing it without counting the attempt (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed the shutdown losing its log output, as Log4j stopped in its own shutdown hook (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed concurrent first calls of DatastoreProvider.getDatastore for a prefix creating a second MongoClient that was never closed (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed an empty secret such as smtp.password: "" failing the startup in prod as a literal secret (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed server sent event connections not registered in the ServerSentEventManager holding the shutdown until application.shutdown.timeout (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed Crypto.encrypt and Crypto.decrypt with a public or private key not rejecting a null key (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed Router.reset not clearing the registered URLs (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed TotpUtils.getOtpAuthURL not encoding name and issuer, which broke the URL for values with spaces or & (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed JwtUtils.parseJwt failing with a NullPointerException instead of a MangooJwtException when exp, iat or nbf is missing (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed MangooUtils.flattenMapHelper not rejecting a null target map (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed Mail.from(name, address) reporting a missing name as missing address and vice versa (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed Mail.textMessage and Mail.htmlMessage with a template not rejecting null content with a clear message (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed TemplateContext writing into the content map of the caller, which failed for immutable maps such as Map.of (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed Authentication.login not writing a cookie while the browser still sent a stale or revoked one (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed the admin security page proposing a TOTP secret that is not Base32 (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed expectTrue, expectFalse, expectNull and expectNotNull having no default error message (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed a missing application.secret failing the startup with a NullPointerException instead of an error message (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed the instance id system property being application.instance.id instead of mangooio.instance.id (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed TestRequest.withBasicAuthentication not sending the credentials (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed the archetype importing Datastore from its old package and setting authentication.redirect instead of authentication.redirect.login (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed the MessageBroker preparing its collection again after a stop and logging a failed instance removal on shutdown as error (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed an unreadable or expired session cookie never being replaced, which failed every CSRF check until the cookie was deleted (svenkubiak)

docs.title: Version 10.15.0
docs.text:
Released at 03.10.2026

  • Behaviour change Session#put and Flash#put reject reserved JWT claim names and internal keys with an IllegalArgumentException instead of losing the whole cookie, the ineffective check for "|", ":", "&" and spaces was removed (svenkubiak)
  • Behaviour change Mail#header rejects a value with line breaks and an invalid header name with an IllegalArgumentException to prevent header injection (svenkubiak)
  • Behaviour change The application refuses to start if a @Run method is not public or has parameters, such a job was scheduled but never ran (svenkubiak)
  • Behaviour change The application refuses to start in prod mode when running as root, the check never applied before as it ran before the mode was set (svenkubiak)
  • Behaviour change Validator#expectNumeric accepts signed decimal numbers with ASCII digits instead of digits only, use expectRegex to require digits only (svenkubiak)
  • Behaviour change The classpath scan on startup skips known library packages, which reduces the startup time, application classes must not be placed in these packages (svenkubiak)
  • Added proxy support for SSE routes: X-Accel-Buffering and Cache-Control headers and a comment heartbeat every 30 seconds (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed Form#getInteger, #getLong, #getDouble and #getFloat throwing a NumberFormatException instead of returning an empty Optional for values the target type cannot parse (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed Validator#expectMinValue, #expectMaxValue and #expectRangeValue throwing on Unicode digits and rejecting negative and decimal numbers (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed Validator#expectExactMatch and #expectMatch accepting an empty value when the other field is filled (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed the HTTP parameter pollution check being bypassable with a percent-encoded parameter name (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed every SSE client receiving a bogus ": ok" data event on connect (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed concurrent login and second factor attempts exceeding the failed attempt budget (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed the startup failing when a class with a @Run method has further annotated methods or the @Run method has further annotations (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed errors of scheduled tasks being swallowed by a NullPointerException instead of being logged (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed runs of an "Every X" job overlapping when a run takes longer than the interval, the next run is now scheduled after the previous one finished (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed the server accepting requests before collections, indexes, jobs and subscribers were registered, which silently dropped saves during startup (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed a mail without from() not being sent, smtp.from is now used as default sender and every send failure is logged (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed an HTML mail with attachments being sent as plain text (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed a NullPointerException when a cache fallback returns null or null is put into the cache, null is now returned and not cached, putting null removes the value (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed Datastore#save not storing an object with an id set by the application but reporting success, save now inserts or replaces (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed MongoDB usernames and passwords with special characters breaking the connection and a missing authdb resulting in authSource=null, credentials are now passed separately and authdb defaults to admin (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed a missing translation key in ${i18n("key")} failing the whole page, it now renders an empty string and is logged once as warning (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed the dev mode failing on a clean build that deletes target/classes, the directory is now watched again once it is recreated (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed the maven archetype failing with -DoutputDirectory or in IDE wizards and leaving the application secret placeholder behind (svenkubiak)
  • Fixed Authentication#isValidLogin not checking the salt, a missing salt consumed a failed login attempt (svenkubiak)
  • Version bumps (svenkubiak)
  • undertow-core 2.4.3.Final -> 2.4.4.Final

Released at 30.09.2026

  • Added an optional ServerSentEventRoute#withHandler(Class) which replaces the default ServerSentEventHandler of an SSE route with a connection callback of the application, so that a connection can be inspected, rejected or keyed per client instead of per request URI, a route without it keeps the previous broadcast behaviour and a custom handler is responsible for registering the connection and for attaching a close task itself (svenkubiak)
  • Added ServerSentEventManager#removeConnection(key, connection) which removes a connection from a given key, as the existing removeConnection(connection) can only find a connection that is held under its request URI (svenkubiak)
  • WebSocketRoute#to now registers itself as type "websocket" instead of "sse", which only affected the startup log and let a URL bound as both a WebSocket and a request route slip through the duplicate detection (svenkubiak)

docs.title: Version 10.13.0
docs.text:
Released at 29.09.2026

  • Behaviour change Argon2 hashing is now gated as an OOM protection since a single computation holds the configured memory cost of heap for its entire duration, the new io.mangoo.crypto.PasswordHasher holds the limit, CommonUtils#hashArgon2 and CommonUtils#matchArgon2 throw an unchecked MangooHashingException when no slot becomes available in time and the ExceptionHandler answers it with 503 instead of 500 (svenkubiak)
  • Added authentication.hashing.concurrency and authentication.hashing.timeout to configure the gate and authentication.hashing.memory, authentication.hashing.iterations and authentication.hashing.parallelism to configure the Argon2 parameters, values below 8192 KiB, 2 iterations or 1 lane are rejected at startup (svenkubiak)
  • Behaviour change The Argon2 defaults are lowered from m=80000, t=6, p=2 to m=32768, t=3, p=1, which is still above the OWASP minimum at around 100 ms and 32 MB instead of 230 ms and 91 MB per hash, p=1 because BouncyCastle computes the lanes sequentially (svenkubiak)
  • Behaviour change CommonUtils#hashArgon2 now returns the standard PHC string $argon2id$v=19$m=...,t=...,p=...$salt$hash instead of a bare Base64 hash, CommonUtils#matchArgon2 verifies with the parameters embedded in the stored hash rather than the current configuration, hashes from earlier versions keep verifying with m=80000, t=6, p=2 and the given salt, and the given salt must still match the one embedded in a PHC hash (svenkubiak)
  • Added CommonUtils#needsRehash(hash) which reports a legacy hash or a hash created with other than the configured parameters, to be evaluated only after a successful verification, so applications can rehash transparently on login (svenkubiak)
  • CommonUtils#matchArgon2 now compares the raw hash bytes in constant time instead of comparing the Base64 representation with a short-circuiting Arrays#areEqual (svenkubiak)
  • Behaviour change Authentication#isValid now means "fully authenticated" and returns false while a second factor is outstanding, the previous behaviour is available as Authentication#hasSubject and Authentication#isValidLogin now fails closed without counting a failed attempt (svenkubiak)
  • Added Authentication#isValidSecondFactor(identifier, secret, totp) which applies the authentication.lock failed attempt budget to the second factor, deprecating the unthrottled Authentication#isValidSecondFactor(secret, totp), and Authentication#userHasSecondFactorLock (svenkubiak)
  • Behaviour change The failed attempt budgets of the password step and the second factor step are now counted separately, a lockout is an absolute point in time, authentication.lock locks on the configured attempt instead of one attempt later and the new authentication.lock.duration configures its duration in minutes (svenkubiak)
  • Added form.maxfilesize to configure the maximum size of a single uploaded file, the default stays at 5 MiB and note that undertow.maxentitysize still caps the whole request body one layer earlier (svenkubiak)
  • The FormHandler now logs on WARN why it rejected a form, including the offending size and the limit, instead of failing the request without a single log line (svenkubiak)

docs.title: Configuration ⚙️
docs.text:
Almost all runtime behavior is controlled through one YAML file: src/main/resources/config.yaml. mangoo I/O loads it with SnakeYAML, flattens the nested keys into dot notation, and exposes them through the Config class and Guice @Named bindings. There is deliberately no second configuration mechanism (no properties files, no XML, no @ConfigurationProperties classes to keep in sync); if a setting exists, it lives in this one file, which makes it realistic to actually read the whole configuration of an application in one sitting.

Typical uses include connector host and port, cookie names, MongoDB connection details, SMTP settings, feature toggles (admin UI, metrics, scheduler), and security options (CORS, authentication redirects). Sensitive values should reference environment variables, JVM properties or secret files rather than plain text in the repository, since config.yaml normally ends up committed to source control.

The file is split into a default block (shared by all modes) and an environments block with overrides for dev, test, and prod. When the application starts, it merges default with the section for the active mode, key by key, so a key you only set in default still applies everywhere, and a key you also set under environments.prod overrides it just for production. Missing an environment section for the active mode causes startup to fail on purpose. That may feel strict the first time it happens, but it exists to catch an environment block that was renamed or forgotten, where the app would otherwise silently fall back to defaults in a place where nobody is watching. Only dev, test and prod exist; any other value of application.mode selects prod.

Values are addressed with dot notation that mirrors the YAML hierarchy:

application:
  api:
    key: foo

config.getString("application.api.key");

You can point the application at a different file entirely by setting the JVM property application.config to an absolute path, which is handy for a config file that lives outside the JAR in production (see Operating).

docs.title: Accessing configuration
docs.text:
Inject io.mangoo.core.Config. Constructor injection is preferred, mostly because it makes Config show up in your test setup explicitly instead of being pulled in behind the scenes:

import io.mangoo.core.Config;
import jakarta.inject.Inject;

public class MyService {
    private final Config config;

    @Inject
    public MyService(Config config) {
        this.config = config;
    }
}

Look up values by key string, or by the constants in io.mangoo.constants.Key if you would rather avoid typos in raw strings scattered across the codebase:

config.getString("application.api.key");
config.getString(Key.APPLICATION_API_KEY);

Typed helpers also exist (getInt, getLong, getBoolean) and dedicated getters such as getApplicationName() or getSmtpHost() for the values the framework itself relies on.

Every entry in config.yaml is also bound as a Guice @Named string, so a class that only needs one particular value can ask for exactly that, rather than pulling in the whole Config object:

@Inject
public MyService(@Named("application.named") String named) {
    // ...
}

docs.title: Modes
docs.text:
mangoo I/O has three modes: dev, test, and prod. The mode decides which environments.<mode> block gets merged into default, so switching modes is really just switching which overrides apply, not a different code path.

  • dev is activated by mvn mangooio:run.
  • test is activated when tests start the application through TestRunner.
  • prod is the default when you start the packaged JAR, so you do not need to set anything special for a normal deployment.

Set the mode explicitly with a system property, useful when you want prod-like behavior locally to reproduce something:

java -Dapplication.mode=dev -jar myapp.jar

or, less common outside of tooling that starts the JVM itself:

System.setProperty("application.mode", "dev");

docs.title: Environment-specific values
docs.text:
Put shared settings under default and overrides under environments.<mode>. The active mode overwrites matching keys from default, leaving everything else untouched:

default:
  application:
    name: myapp
    url: http://localhost

environments:
  test:
    application:
      url: https://test.example.com
  prod:
    application:
      url: https://example.com

Here application.name stays myapp in every mode, since none of the environment blocks touch it, while application.url changes depending on where the app is actually running.

The active environment block is required, even if it only overrides a single key. If environments.dev (or test / prod) is missing entirely, startup fails rather than quietly falling back to default alone.

docs.title: Secrets, environment variables, and JVM arguments
docs.text:
Configuration values can also come from environment variables, JVM arguments or secret files instead of being written out in plain text. See Secrets for how env{}, arg{} and file{} placeholders are resolved. A placeholder without a value and without a fallback fails the startup, unless it is optional (env{?}), and in prod mode the framework secrets must not be literal.

As a rule of thumb: cookie secrets and keys, database and SMTP credentials should never sit in source control as clear text, since config.yaml is versioned right alongside your application code and gets the same read access as everything else in the repository.

docs.title: Connectors
docs.text:
At least one HTTP or HTTPS connector must be configured, otherwise the application refuses to start. There is no implicit port. A connector starts only when both host and port are set. HTTPS accepts TLS 1.3 only.

default:
  connector:
    http:
      host: localhost
      port: 8080
    https:
      host: localhost
      port: 8443
      keystore: /etc/myapp/https.p12
      password: file{}

HTTPS reads key and certificate chain from the PKCS12 file in connector.https.keystore, see Secrets. connector.https.certificate.alias is only needed if the file holds more than one key entry.
