docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
Production systems need visibility beyond log lines. mangoo I/O exposes request metrics (counts and latency) for the admin dashboard and optional OpenTelemetry export for traces and metrics. Both are off by default so local development stays lightweight; enable them explicitly when you deploy.

The dashboard metrics answer "how much traffic and how slow?" for the instance that serves the page. OTLP sends spans and metrics out to a collector (Jaeger, Grafana Tempo, Prometheus via the OpenTelemetry Collector, vendor backends), where the data of all instances comes together. See Operating for JVM and secrets setup alongside these features.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Set metrics.enable to true to start counting requests and recording processing time. Values show up on the admin dashboard. Metrics stay off by default so they never add overhead you did not ask for.

metrics:
  enable: true

Requests whose URI contains @admin are excluded. Health probes never reach the counter, because they are handled before it. User SSE and WebSocket routes have no route template and are stored under their request path for the whole connection lifetime. At most 1000 route templates are kept. The rest are Other routes. Errors are status codes of 500 and above. Times on the dashboard are milliseconds.

docs.title: OpenTelemetry
docs.text:
mangoo I/O can export traces and metrics over OTLP/gRPC:

otlp:
  enable: true
  endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:4317

When enabled, spans and metrics go out with these resource attributes:

Attribute Value service.name application.name service.instance.id the instance id, hostname with a random suffix framework.name, framework.version io.mangoo and its version framework.environment the application mode

Every request is recorded in the histogram http.server.request.duration (seconds, attributes http.request.method and http.response.status_code). Buckets run from 0.005 to 10 seconds. Health probes are outside the telemetry handler. A response whose Content-Type starts with text/event-stream is skipped. WebSocket exchanges are not. The span name is the raw request path, plus a child span Invoke controller. When otlp.enable is true, MongoDB commands are traced as well.

service.name is application.name (default mangooio-application). framework.environment is PROD, DEV, or TEST. Export uses the SDK default interval of the periodic reader, 60 seconds in the OpenTelemetry Java version this build uses, and once more on shutdown. Leave otlp.enable false unless a collector is listening. The endpoint is gRPC, for example http://127.0.0.1:4317.

For load balancer and orchestrator probes use /@health/live and /@health/ready, see Operating. If you need a MongoDB ping for your own checks, call Datastore.isHealthy() directly.

docs.title: Operating
docs.text:
mangoo I/O applications ship as a fat JAR built with the Maven shade plugin. One process runs Undertow, your controllers, and the scheduler, so there is no separate WAR deployment step. Production runs use Java 25 and prod mode, against an external MongoDB. Embedded MongoDB still starts in prod, but the application logs a warning: each instance gets its own database and shares no lockouts, revocations, or events with the others.

Secrets come from the host through env{}, arg{}, or file{}. In prod mode the application refuses to start when a framework secret is written literally into the config.yaml on the classpath. A file passed with -Dapplication.config is not checked that way. Empty values pass. A fallback written inside env{...} still counts as a literal. The checked keys are application.secret, application.admin.secret, application.api.key, the session, authentication, and flash cookie secrets and keys, smtp.password, connector.https.password, and any persistence.*.mongo.password. application.admin.password is an Argon2 hash and is not in that list. The YAML shape is the same in every environment; what changes is the active block and where the secret values come from.

Run the packaged application:

java -Dapplication.mode=prod -jar myapp.jar

Provide the secrets in production, for example as environment variables for keys set to env{}:

export APPLICATION_SECRET='exactly-64-bytes................................................'
export SESSION_COOKIE_SECRET='exactly-64-bytes................................................'
java -Dapplication.mode=prod -jar /opt/myapp/myapp.jar

java -jar starts in prod mode. -Dapplication.mode accepts dev and test, case-insensitively. Any other value, including staging, is prod. mvn mangooio:run forces dev mode on the child process.

Configure at least one HTTP or HTTPS connector. A connector starts only when both host and port are set. Zero connectors exits the process. HTTPS reads a PKCS12 file from connector.https.keystore and speaks TLS 1.3 only. The alias is required only when the file has more than one key entry.

On an operating system whose name does not start with Windows, prod mode runs id -u and exits when the uid is 0. Run the process as an unprivileged user, and give that user read access to the secrets directory if you use file{}. If id is missing, the failure is logged and startup continues.

docs.title: Startup and classpath scanning
docs.text: On startup the classpath is scanned for @Run jobs, @Collection models and Subscriber implementations, so these classes can live in any package of your application. Known library packages such as org.apache, com.google, io.undertow or com.mongodb are excluded from the scan to keep the startup fast, therefore do not place application classes in these packages. The excluded packages are logged on debug level.

docs.title: Supervisord
docs.text:
[program:myapp]
command=/usr/bin/java -Dapplication.mode=prod -jar /opt/myapp/myapp.jar
directory=/opt/myapp
autostart=true
autorestart=true
stderr_logfile=/var/log/myapp.err.log
stdout_logfile=/var/log/myapp.out.log
user=myuser
environment=JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-Xms512m -Xmx1024m",APPLICATION_SECRETS_PATH="/etc/myapp/secrets"

Note that JAVA_OPTS set in environment= is not read by java unless you also put it on the command line yourself. JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, by contrast, is picked up automatically.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
FROM eclipse-temurin:25-jre
RUN groupadd --system --gid 10001 app && useradd --system --uid 10001 --gid app app
WORKDIR /app
COPY target/myapp.jar myapp.jar
USER app
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-Dapplication.mode=prod", "-jar", "/app/myapp.jar"]

Containers run as root unless the image or the compose file sets a user. Keep the USER line. On an image that has id and starts as uid 0, prod mode exits. Pass heap settings through JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS. Docker secrets land in /run/secrets, which is the default directory for file{}. Override it with APPLICATION_SECRETS_PATH or -Dapplication.secrets.path. A secret file may be at most 64 KiB, and a trailing newline is stripped. See Secrets for the compose file, config.yaml, and permissions.

Environment variables with env{} work as well, preferably with --env-file rather than -e, but stay visible in docker inspect and to every child process.

docs.title: Health checks
docs.text:
Two endpoints answer load balancer and orchestrator probes. They sit in front of metrics, cookies, and filters, return no body, send Cache-Control: no-store, and need no configuration. Only GET and HEAD are probes. Any other method falls through to normal routing. Security headers are not added.

Endpoint 200 503 /@health/live the connector accepts the connection, including during shutdown - /@health/ready startup has finished during startup and from the first step of shutdown

Readiness flips to true only after Undertow is listening, the shutdown hook is registered, Datastore.isHealthy() has succeeded, and applicationStarted() has returned. Before the port listens, a probe fails at TCP, not with 503.

MongoDB is not part of the readiness flag. If persistence is on (the default) and the ping fails, the process exits 1 after the port is already open, while readiness is still 503. persistence.enable: false makes isHealthy() return true without a client. A MongoDB outage after startup does not take the instance out of rotation. If it did, every instance would fail the probe at once and the load balancer would have nowhere to send traffic.

The port in the sample below is 8080, the archetype default. The generated environments.dev, test, and prod blocks set the port to 9090. Probe the port you actually bind.

livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /@health/live
    port: 8080
readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /@health/ready
    port: 8080

docs.title: Graceful shutdown
docs.text:
On SIGTERM or SIGINT the JVM shutdown hook runs, in this order:

  1. Reports not ready on /@health/ready and starts the shutdown clock.
  2. Stops the admin heartbeat. That step is capped at 2 seconds, so a dead MongoDB does not hold the shutdown. A failed delete leaves the row in mangooio_instances until expireAt, one minute after the last heartbeat.
  3. Stops scheduling further @Run tasks. A task that is already running is not interrupted yet.
  4. Closes SSE connections, including /@admin/stream, and WebSocket connections (GOING_AWAY, reason Server shutdown). Clients reconnect to another instance.
  5. Answers new requests with 503 and waits for the ones already in flight, using whatever is left of the deadline.
  6. Stops Undertow, then waits for running @Run tasks. At the deadline those tasks are interrupted. The log lines are Open requests did not finish within application.shutdown.timeout and Scheduled tasks did not finish within application.shutdown.timeout and are interrupted.
  7. Stops the MessageBroker and calls applicationStopped() while the MongoDB clients are still open.
  8. Closes the clients, stops embedded MongoDB if it was started, flushes OpenTelemetry (5 seconds), and stops Log4j. Log4j's own shutdown hook is disabled so this order holds.

application.shutdown.timeout is 20 seconds by default and starts at step 1, so the heartbeat stop and the connection close already consume it. A negative value is treated as 0. The application does not wait for the load balancer to notice that the instance is going away. Add that delay in front, for example with a Kubernetes preStop hook, and keep terminationGracePeriodSeconds above preStop plus application.shutdown.timeout:

terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 40
containers:
  - name: myapp
    lifecycle:
      preStop:
        sleep:
          seconds: 10

docs.title: Running several instances
docs.text:
Several instances of one application can run behind a load balancer. Session data and the CSRF token live in the session cookie. A kept form lives in the flash cookie. Both cookies, and the authentication cookie, are encrypted and signed JWTs, so a request can reach any instance. Every instance needs the same secrets, the same cookie names, and the same application.name, which is the JWT issuer.

Every instance logs its id at startup: HOSTNAME if that variable is set, otherwise the host part of the JVM runtime name, plus a dash and six hex characters. The admin dashboard and the OpenTelemetry resource (service.instance.id) carry the same id. Add it to the log pattern with ${sys:mangooio.instance.id}, see Logging. Dashboard metrics are per instance. OpenTelemetry metrics are aggregated by the collector, see Observability.

  • Secrets. Pass them with env{}, arg{}, or file{}. See Secrets.
  • Clocks. Cookies are checked against the clock of the instance that receives them, with 30 seconds of skew on exp, nbf, and iat. New tokens are issued with nbf set 30 seconds in the past. Keep the clocks in sync with NTP.
  • MongoDB. Use one external MongoDB for all instances. Embedded MongoDB starts a separate database per instance, and prod mode only warns about that. A replica set or sharded cluster is persistence.mongo.url. See Persistence. MongoDB older than 4.2 fails startup. Framework collections use a primary read preference and majority write concern, whatever the connection string says. Application queries on Datastore do not.
  • Scheduler. @Run runs on every instance. A job that must run once has no @Run. Expose it as a route protected with ApiKeyFilter and call it from an external trigger, such as a Kubernetes CronJob, through the load balancer. A retry after a timeout runs the job again, so keep it idempotent and answer a long job with 202. Set scheduler.enable: false only when no job should run on the instances. Overlapping runs of the same job do not happen: the next run is scheduled after the previous one finishes. The first run waits for the full interval. It does not run at startup.
  • Startup logic. applicationStarted() runs on every instance. Migrations and seed data have to tolerate concurrent runs. The port is already open while that method runs. Readiness stays 503 until it returns, which keeps a probe from sending traffic, but a client that already knows the address can arrive before the seed inserts.
  • Cache. The application cache is local to each instance. Bind your own Cache if entries or counters must be shared.
  • EventBus. Subscribers run on the instance that published the event, one after another on a single virtual thread. The publisher is not blocked. The next subscriber is.
  • Server-Sent Events. ServerSentEventManager.send delivers to local connections and, when persistence is on, inserts into the capped collection mangooio_messages (16 MiB). Other instances tail that collection from the end. There is no replay. A failed insert means the other instances never see the event. The connections stay on the instance that accepted them.
  • WebSockets. The framework holds the connections and closes them on shutdown. There is no fan-out. Publish on io.mangoo.interfaces.MessageBroker and subscribe on each instance to forward to its own channels. SSE and WebSocket routes are public: no authentication, no filters, no CSRF. See Routing.
  • Authentication state. Failed logins, used TOTP codes, and the pending admin second factor are shared through MongoDB (mangooio_attempts, mangooio_claims) when persistence is on. If MongoDB is down, a login or a second factor is refused. Revocation of authentication cookies is separate and off by default. Set authentication.blacklist to store revocations in mangooio_revocations and to reject a revoked cookie. With the default false, a MongoDB outage does not invalidate cookies that are already issued. In-memory stores, used when persistence.enable is false, are wiped on restart: a lock or a revocation is forgotten. See Framework collections.
  • Admin dashboard. Every instance reports every ten seconds while the dashboard is enabled. The list shows the last heartbeat of each instance. An instance with no heartbeat for 30 seconds is marked stale and drops out of the list after a minute. Cache clear and metrics reset are published on the MessageBroker and run on every instance. The blocks under the instance list are the instance that served the page. Request counts stay at zero unless metrics.enable is true, and the error count is HTTP 5xx only.
  • Indexes. A changed @Indexed definition fails index creation and the new instance does not start. During a rolling deploy, drop the old index before the new version starts. persistence.mongo.schema: validate creates nothing and exits with the mongosh commands that are missing.

docs.title: Reverse proxy
docs.text: connector.proxy: true inserts Undertow's proxy-peer handler, so the client address and Request.getScheme() follow X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto. The default is false. Turn it on only when every request passes a proxy that overwrites X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Proto, X-Forwarded-Host, and X-Forwarded-Port. Otherwise a client can set any address.

docs.title: Cookies
docs.text:
Session, authentication, flash, and locale cookies are HttpOnly and Path=/. Session and authentication SameSite must be Strict or Lax. Anything else, including None, fails startup. Flash and the locale cookie are always Strict. Secure defaults to false for session and authentication. The flash cookie follows session.cookie.secure. There is no flash.cookie.secure key. The archetype writes one, and it is ignored.

Startup logs a warning, also shown on the admin dashboard, when Secure is false, when a cookie name is still the default (mangooio-auth, mangooio-session, mangooio-flash), or when a cookie secret or key equals application.secret. The warning is logged in every mode.

There is no sliding session expiry. Rewriting the session cookie keeps the original exp.

The admin cookie is documented in Administration. In prod it is named __Host-mangooio-admin and is Secure, so a deployment on plain HTTP will not keep the operator signed in.

docs.title: Request size
docs.text:
These limits are applied before a controller runs:

Limit Default Configurable undertow.maxentitysize 4 MiB (4194304) yes Undertow parameters 1000 no Undertow header size 8192 bytes no form.maxfilesize 5 MiB per file yes Form files 10 no Form parameters 1000 no Form value length 10 000 characters no Flash cookie name plus value 4096 bytes no

Worker and I/O thread counts are Undertow's own defaults. The framework does not set them.

A form that exceeds the file, parameter, or value limits throws before the controller runs. The response is HTTP 400. An HTML client still receives the built-in 500 page. A JSON Content-Type receives {"error":"<reason>"}. The body is rejected earlier by undertow.maxentitysize, which at the default of 4 MiB is smaller than form.maxfilesize. Raise the body limit before a 5 MiB upload can succeed, and raise the proxy's body limit as well.

smtp.protocol: smtp fails startup in prod. smtps and smtptls are allowed. Connect and read timeouts default to 10 seconds and 30 seconds. 0 is rejected. Argon2 concurrency, memory, and the 503 returned when every hashing slot is busy are described in Configuration.

docs.title: Global response headers
docs.text:
Controller responses, the 404 fallback, error pages, and authentication redirects send:

Header Value X-Content-Type-Options nosniff X-Frame-Options DENY X-XSS-Protection 1 Referrer-Policy no-referrer Server Undertow

Content-Security-Policy and Feature-Policy are registered as empty strings and are not sent until you set a non-blank value. A blank value is dropped.

These headers are not applied to SSE, WebSocket handshakes, static files from Bind.pathResource() and Bind.fileResource(), or the early 400 for a repeated query key or, with application.parameter.strict, a query key that collides with a path parameter.

Override or add to them in Bootstrap:

import io.mangoo.constants.Header;
import io.mangoo.core.Server;

Server.header(Header.CONTENT_SECURITY_POLICY, "default-src 'self'");

docs.title: Maven plugin
docs.text:
mvn mangooio:run

The plugin does not compile. It watches target/classes (and any extra directories you configure) and restarts a child JVM after the files settle. The settle delay is mangoo.settleDownMillis, default 500 ms. The child is io.mangoo.core.Application with -Dapplication.mode=dev. Optional mangoo.jvmArgs, and mangoo.jpdaPort for JDWP with suspend=n. A port of 0, the default, opens no debugger.

templates/**/*.ftl, *.less, *.sass, and assets/** are excluded from the watch. In dev mode Freemarker reloads a template about once a second, so a template change does not need a process restart. The shade plugin that builds the fat JAR is in the archetype POM, not a goal of this plugin. There is no framework Docker image.

See Observability for metrics and tracing, and Logging for Log4j.

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text:
mangoo I/O includes a thin integration layer over the MongoDB Java Sync Driver. You work with POJOs and BSON queries directly, there is no ORM query language on top and no Morphia (it was removed in 8.0).

At startup, the framework scans for classes annotated with @Collection, registers their collection names, and optionally creates indexes from @Indexed fields. Inject Datastore (or DatastoreProvider when you need multiple databases) and use familiar driver patterns: save, find, findAll, and query() for fluent, driver-level access.

For local development, the archetype can start embedded MongoDB 7.0 when persistence.mongo.embedded is true, so you get a working database with zero setup. Turn that off in production and point host / port, or a url, at your actual MongoDB server. Passwords belong in the environment or a secret file, never in source control.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
default:
  persistence:
    mongo:
      host: 127.0.0.1
      port: 27017
      username: myUsername
      password: env{}
      dbname: myDBname
      authdb: myAuthDB
      auth: true
      embedded: false

Set persistence.enable to false if you want to skip MongoDB entirely; the framework then keeps its own state in memory, see Framework collections.

host and port address one server. A replica set, several mongos instances, or an SRV address such as MongoDB Atlas goes into url, which then replaces host and port:

persistence:
  mongo:
    url: mongodb://mongo-1:27017,mongo-2:27017/?replicaSet=rs0
    username: myUsername
    password: env{}
    dbname: myDBname
    authdb: admin
    auth: true

url accepts any connection string the driver supports, including mongodb+srv://cluster.example.mongodb.net. Options in the query string, such as replicaSet, tls, retryWrites and w, are passed through. The database mangoo I/O uses is still dbname. If the URL contains a database or authSource, that value has to match dbname or authdb, and startup fails when it does not. An omitted authdb means admin. Credentials in the URL are rejected, so username, password and authdb stay in the keys above and special characters need no URL encoding. url cannot be combined with embedded: true, because the embedded server is started from host and port only.

Note

persistence.mongo.embedded: true starts MongoDB 7.0 in-process. Use it only for local development and tests, never in production.

There is no package setting to configure. Just annotate your entity classes and Classgraph finds them on its own.

docs.title: Entities
docs.text:
import io.mangoo.annotations.Collection;
import io.mangoo.annotations.Indexed;
import io.mangoo.enums.Sort;
import io.mangoo.persistence.Entity;

@Collection(name = "people")
public class Person extends Entity {
    @Indexed(sort = Sort.ASCENDING, unique = true)
    private String email;

    private String firstname;
    private String lastname;
}

Entity stores _id as a BSON ObjectId. Extending it is optional as long as you implement BaseEntity yourself instead.

@Indexed is applied at startup. It understands sort, unique, and caseSensitive. caseSensitive = false builds an index with an English collation at secondary strength (locale "en"), not a generic case-insensitive index. The index key is the Java field name. Embedded MongoDB 7.0 starts only for the default persistence. prefix, in the module constructor. DatastoreProvider.getDatastore(String) does not start an embedded server for a named prefix. persistence.mongo.url together with embedded MongoDB fails startup.

docs.title: Datastore
docs.text:
import io.mangoo.interfaces.persistence.Datastore;
import jakarta.inject.Inject;

public class PersonService {
    private final Datastore datastore;

    @Inject
    public PersonService(Datastore datastore) {
        this.datastore = datastore;
    }
}

import static com.mongodb.client.model.Filters.eq;

String id = datastore.save(person);
Person found = datastore.find(Person.class, eq("_id", new ObjectId(id)));
List<Person> all = datastore.findAll(Person.class);
long count = datastore.countAll(Person.class);
datastore.delete(person);
datastore.dropCollection(Person.class);
datastore.isHealthy();

countAll returns -1 when the count fails. saveAll calls save once per element. It is not a bulk write. getMongoClient() and getMongoDatabase() hand you the driver. query(String) and query(String, Class) do the same for a collection. dropDatabase() drops the database of this datastore.

save inserts an object without an id and replaces the document of an object with an id. An object whose id was set by the application, e.g. to reference it before it is stored, is inserted under that id if no document exists yet. The generated id of an inserted object is returned, but not written back to the object, so load it again before changing and saving it a second time.

Query helpers:

Person first = datastore.findFirst(Person.class, Sorts.descending("created"));
List<Person> page = datastore.findAll(Person.class, Filters.eq("active", true), Sorts.ascending("lastname"), 50);

When you need the full driver API rather than the convenience helpers, drop down to query():

List<Booking> bookings = new ArrayList<>();
datastore
    .query(Booking.class)
    .find(Filters.and(
        Filters.gte("booked", fromDate),
        Filters.lte("booked", toDate)))
    .into(bookings);

Index helpers cover addIndex, dropIndex, and dropAllIndexes. saveAll calls save for each element of a list (no bulk write, not atomic), and getMongoDatabase() hands you the native driver handle for anything not covered above.

docs.title: Multiple connections
docs.text:
@Inject
public PersonService(DatastoreProvider datastoreProvider) {
    this.readonly = datastoreProvider.getDatastore("readonly");
}

The prefix you pass to getDatastore maps directly to persistence.<prefix>.mongo.*:

persistence:
  readonly:
    mongo:
      host: 127.0.0.1
      port: 27017
      username: reader
      password: env{}
      dbname: myDBname
      authdb: myAuthDB
      auth: true
      embedded: false

docs.title: Framework collections
docs.text:
With persistence enabled, the framework keeps the state that all instances have to share in the default datastore, i.e. in the database of persistence.mongo.dbname, next to the collections of your application. Give every application its own dbname: two applications in one database would share these collections, so a lock of one user name would apply to both and server sent events would reach the clients of the other application.

Collection Store Content mangooio_attempts AttemptStore Failed login budgets and locks mangooio_claims OneTimeStore Used TOTP codes and the pending second factor of the admin login mangooio_revocations TokenBlacklist Revoked authentication cookies (authentication.blacklist) mangooio_messages MessageBroker Server sent events and admin actions for the other instances, capped at 16 MB mangooio_instances InstanceRegistry Heartbeat of every instance for the admin dashboard

The startup creates them: a TTL index on expireAt for mangooio_attempts, mangooio_claims, mangooio_revocations and mangooio_instances, which removes expired entries, and the capped collection mangooio_messages. A mangooio_messages that exists but is not capped fails the startup. After the database was dropped, for example in tests, the indexes are created again on the next start. The database user needs the built-in role readWrite on dbname, which covers creating collections and indexes. See Schema for a user without that right. MongoDB 4.2 or later is required. Reads go to the primary and writes are acknowledged by the majority, whatever url sets.

If MongoDB is unavailable, AttemptStore and OneTimeStore fail closed: a login or a second factor is refused. TokenBlacklist.isRevoked is consulted only when authentication.blacklist is true. With the default false, an existing authentication cookie keeps working during an outage. When the blacklist is on, a MongoDB error counts the cookie as revoked. See Operating.

Without persistence the same state is kept in memory per process. It is lost on a restart, so a revoked cookie that has not yet expired is accepted again, and a lock or used TOTP code is forgotten. This is fine for a single instance that can accept it; several instances always need persistence. persistence.enable switches the datastore and the framework state together, there is no separate switch: an application that does not use the Datastore itself still gets the shared state with persistence enabled. To keep the state elsewhere, bind your own implementation of the store in app.Module.

docs.title: Schema
docs.text:
persistence.mongo.schema controls whether the startup creates the collections and indexes of the default datastore: the @Indexed indexes of your entities and the framework collections.

Value Behaviour create Creates missing collections and indexes (default) validate Creates nothing and checks that everything exists; the startup fails with a list of the missing parts as mongosh commands

Use validate when the database user may not create collections or indexes, e.g. because a DBA manages the schema. Run the listed commands once with a user that may, then start again:

persistence.mongo.schema is validate, but the database lacks the following, create it with mongosh:
  db.getCollection("mangooio_attempts").createIndex({"expireAt": 1}, {"expireAfterSeconds": 0})
  db.createCollection("mangooio_messages", {"capped": true, "size": 16777216})

An index counts as present if its keys, uniqueness, collation and expiry match. Without the TTL indexes expired entries would never be removed, which is why a missing one fails the startup instead of logging a warning. With validate, a mangooio_messages that is dropped while the application runs is not created again; the server sent events of the other instances pause until it exists.

docs.title: Routing 🧭
docs.text:
Routing connects incoming URLs to controller methods. In mangoo I/O every route is declared in code, typically in app.Bootstrap.initializeRoutes(), so the URL map always matches what is actually compiled into the application. There is no separate routes file that can silently drift out of sync with the controller it is supposed to point at.

You use two builders:

  • On: HTTP verb and path for a controller method, for example On.get().to("/users").respondeWith("list").
  • Bind: Groups routes for a controller, or registers static files, SSE endpoints, and WebSockets.

Once a route matches, the framework invokes the corresponding method on a Guice-managed controller instance. Path segments in {braces} become method parameters, see Controllers for how those get bound.

import controllers.ApplicationController;
import io.mangoo.routing.Bind;
import io.mangoo.routing.On;

@Override
public void initializeRoutes() {
    Bind.controller(ApplicationController.class).withRoutes(
        On.get().to("/").respondeWith("index")
    );
}

A GET request to / calls ApplicationController.index().

Note

The method name on the route builder is respondeWith (with an "e"). It looks like a typo the first time you see it, but it is the actual public API, so autocomplete will not save you here.

A route with a path parameter looks like this:

Bind.controller(UserController.class).withRoutes(
    On.get().to("/users/{id}").respondeWith("show")
);

public Response show(long id) {
    return Response.ok().render("id", id);
}

docs.title: HTTP methods
docs.text:
On.get()
On.post()
On.put()
On.patch()
On.delete()
On.options()
On.head()
On.anyOf(Http.PUT, Http.PATCH, Http.DELETE)

On.anyOf(...) binds one controller method to several verbs at once, useful when the same handler legitimately needs to react to more than one, for example a PUT/PATCH pair that both update a resource but differ only in whether the body is a full or partial representation.

docs.title: Long-running requests
docs.text:
POST, PUT, and PATCH already leave Undertow's I/O thread before the controller runs, body and all. GET, HEAD, DELETE, and OPTIONS stay on the I/O thread unless you mark the route. A slow read on that thread holds up other requests on the same thread. withNonBlocking() dispatches those verbs onto Undertow's worker threads. The name describes the I/O threads you are keeping free, not the work inside the method:

Bind.controller(ApplicationController.class).withRoutes(
    On.get().to("/export").respondeWith("export").withNonBlocking()
);

You can also apply that to every route of a controller at once:

Bind.controller(ExportController.class).withNonBlocking().withRoutes(
    On.get().to("/export").respondeWith("index")
);

Calling it on On.post(), On.put(), or On.patch() changes nothing. Those verbs are dispatched either way. A slow GET without it does not fail. Other requests on that I/O thread wait behind it.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Require a valid authentication cookie on a controller or on a single route. See Authentication for how the cookie itself gets issued and verified.

Bind.controller(DashboardController.class).withAuthentication().withRoutes(
    On.get().to("/dashboard").respondeWith("index")
);

Bind.controller(LoginController.class).withRoutes(
    On.get().to("/account").respondeWith("account").withAuthentication(),
    On.get().to("/login").respondeWith("login")
);

Putting withAuthentication() on the controller protects every route it declares; putting it on a single route lets one controller mix public and protected pages, like the LoginController example above, where /login has to stay reachable by definition.

docs.title: Static files
docs.text:
Files under src/main/resources/files are served once you bind them explicitly:

Bind.pathResource().to("/assets/");
Bind.fileResource().to("/robots.txt");

That maps to:

src/main/resources/files/assets/
src/main/resources/files/robots.txt

pathResource() serves a directory tree. The prefix is forced to start and end with /, and the files are read from the classpath directory files plus that prefix. fileResource() maps one file and is registered as GET only. Nothing under files/ is served unless you bind it. These routes skip authentication, filters, CSRF, and Server.header(...).

docs.title: Server-Sent Events
docs.text:
SSE routes do not use a controller at all, since there is no request/response cycle to hand off to one:

Bind.serverSentEvent().to("/sse");

An SSE route optionally takes its own Undertow ServerSentEventConnectionCallback, which replaces the default handler and lets the application inspect, reject, or individually key a connection as it is established:

Bind.serverSentEvent().to("/sse/client").withHandler(MyServerSentEventHandler.class);

See Server-Sent Events for how to push data to connected clients afterward, and for what a custom handler has to take care of itself.

SSE and WebSocket routes are not authenticated

Both are registered directly on Undertow's path handler, which means they never pass through the handler chain described above. withAuthentication() does not exist on them, and no filter, authentication check, or CSRF protection applies. Anyone who knows the URL can connect.

A custom connection handler is the place to check a token and refuse the handshake. Without that, anything you send is public. Keep user-specific data on a controller route.

docs.title: WebSockets
docs.text:
WebSocket routes use an Undertow WebSocketConnectionCallback directly, rather than a mangoo I/O abstraction on top of it:

Bind.webSocket().to("/ws").withHandler(MyWebSocketHandler.class);

withHandler is required. The handler class is created by Guice, and a missing handler fails startup. There is no test helper for WebSockets or SSE. The handler has to read the authentication cookie off the handshake itself. Connections are tracked and closed on shutdown. There is no cross-instance fan-out. If a message has to reach clients on other instances, publish it on MessageBroker and forward it from the subscriber on each instance. See Operating.

docs.title: Scheduler
docs.text:
Background jobs run inside the same JVM as your web app, no separate Quartz XML or system cron daemon required. Annotate any public method without parameters with @Run and a schedule expression (the application refuses to start otherwise), and Classgraph discovers those methods at startup as long as scheduler.enable is true, which it is by default.

Use fixed-delay expressions such as Every 3m or Every 1d for recurring work like cleanup tasks, cache warming, or report generation. Jobs share Guice injection with the rest of the application, so you can inject services and Datastore exactly like you would in a controller.

docs.title: Fixed delay
docs.text:
import io.mangoo.annotations.Run;

public class InfoJob {
    @Run(at = "Every 3m")
    public void execute() {
        // task
    }
}

Units after Every:

  • s seconds (Every 5s)
  • m minutes (Every 15m)
  • h hours (Every 4h)
  • d days (Every 1d)

The Every prefix is case-insensitive, so every and Every both work.

The interval is the delay between the end of one run and the start of the next. Runs of the same job do not overlap, and the first run waits for the full interval. It does not fire at startup. Cron jobs follow the same rule: the next slot is scheduled after the current run finishes. Cron uses the JVM default zone. application.timezone is applied when the Guice module is constructed, so read the zone after that, not from a static initializer that ran earlier.

docs.title: Cron
docs.text:
Use a 5-field UNIX cron expression: minute, hour, day-of-month, month, day-of-week.

public class NightlyJob {
    @Run(at = "0 2 * * *")
    public void execute() {
        // 02:00 every day
    }
}

This is not Quartz cron; notably, there is no seconds field.

Each run is submitted to a new platform thread. The timer that waits out the delay is a single thread. There is no bounded pool. Disable scheduling entirely with:

scheduler:
  enable: false

docs.title: Secrets 🔐
docs.text:
Production applications need secrets that must never end up in the artifact or in git: cookie secrets and keys, database passwords, SMTP credentials. mangoo I/O reads them from outside the JAR with three placeholders you write directly into config.yaml:

Placeholder Source env{} Operating-system environment variable arg{} JVM system property (-D...) file{} File in the secrets directory, as Kubernetes Secrets and Docker secrets provide them

Every placeholder accepts a fallback in the braces, env{fallback}, which is used only if the source has no value. A placeholder without a value and without a fallback fails the startup and names the key, so a missing secret is noticed at deploy time and not on the first request. Use fallbacks only for values that are not secret; a secret written as fallback sits in config.yaml again.

For a value that may be missing, write env{?}, arg{?} or file{?}. If the source is not set or empty, the key stays unset, as if it were not in config.yaml, and the default of the framework applies. An empty source never replaces a default with an empty string, so an empty SMTP_PROTOCOL keeps smtps and an empty PERSISTENCE_MONGO_URL falls back to host and port:

smtp:
  host: env{?}
  username: env{?}
  password: env{?}
persistence:
  mongo:
    url: env{?}

To find out whether an optional value was given, read it without a default, for example config.getString(Key.SMTP_HOST), which returns null while getSmtpHost() returns the default localhost.

Mounted secret files are the safest of the three sources: environment variables are visible in /proc/<pid>/environ, docker inspect and the pod spec and are inherited by child processes, a file on a tmpfs mount is not.

docs.title: Secrets in prod
docs.text:
In prod mode the framework secrets must come from one of the placeholders. A literal value in the config.yaml on the classpath fails the startup:

  • application.secret, application.admin.secret, application.api.key
  • session.cookie.secret / .key, authentication.cookie.secret / .key, flash.cookie.secret / .key
  • persistence.mongo.password and persistence.<prefix>.mongo.password, smtp.password
  • connector.https.password

A fallback in the braces counts as literal, an empty value does not, as it holds no secret. A config.yaml passed with -Dapplication.config lives outside the JAR and may contain literal values. application.admin.password is an Argon2id hash and may stay literal. In dev and test literal values are allowed, a project created with the archetype ships generated secrets for both.

The cookie secrets and keys fall back to application.secret, so the minimal prod setup is a single APPLICATION_SECRET. application.secret is always required, even if every cookie has dedicated values; the startup warns as long as a cookie uses it, as dedicated values per cookie are recommended.

docs.title: Secret and key length
docs.text:
The cookie secrets (*.cookie.secret) and application.secret are used directly as encryption key for dir with A256CBC_HS512. That algorithm accepts a key of exactly 512 bit, so these values must be exactly 64 bytes long — not more, not less. Bytes count, not characters: a non-ASCII character such as ä takes two bytes in UTF-8. The cookie keys (*.cookie.key) are used for HS512 signing and must be at least 64 bytes, as must application.api.key. The application refuses to start if a value does not meet these rules.

Generate a value with 64 ASCII characters, for example:

LC_ALL=C tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 64

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
Use env{} to read a value from the process environment. The environment name is the config key in uppercase with dots replaced by underscores:

session:
  cookie:
    secret: env{}

This reads SESSION_COOKIE_SECRET.

docs.title: JVM arguments
docs.text:
Use arg{} to read a JVM system property with the same dotted key:

application:
  db:
    username: arg{}

java -Dapplication.db.username=myuser -jar myapp.jar

docs.title: Secret files
docs.text:
Use file{} to read a value from a file named like the key in the secrets directory:

session:
  cookie:
    secret: file{}

This reads /run/secrets/session.cookie.secret. The directory is /run/secrets, the default of Docker secrets, and can be changed with the environment variable APPLICATION_SECRETS_PATH or the JVM property application.secrets.path; it can not be set in config.yaml, as the files are read while config.yaml is resolved.

  • The file name is the key as is; Kubernetes and Docker allow dots in secret names.
  • Symbolic links are followed, as Kubernetes mounts secrets through them.
  • One trailing line break (\n or \r\n) is removed, as files written with echo end with one. Everything else is kept byte for byte.
  • Files larger than 64 KiB are rejected.
  • A file that exists but can not be read fails the startup with the key and the reason, e.g. missing permissions.
  • file{} reads the same directory in every mode. On a development machine there is usually no /run/secrets, so use file{} in the prod section only, or set APPLICATION_SECRETS_PATH in the run configuration of the IDE to a local directory.

Kubernetes:

volumes:
  - name: secrets
    secret:
      secretName: myapp
containers:
  - name: myapp
    volumeMounts:
      - name: secrets
        mountPath: /run/secrets
        readOnly: true

The keys of the Secret myapp are the config keys, e.g. session.cookie.secret.

docs.title: Docker Compose
docs.text: With Compose the secrets are files in one directory on the host, mounted read-only as /run/secrets into the container. /run/secrets is the default secrets directory, so APPLICATION_SECRETS_PATH is not needed.

docs.title: Creating the secret files
docs.text:
Keep the files in a directory next to compose.yaml, e.g. ./secrets, and add it to .gitignore. Name each file like the config key:

File Content Create with application.secret exactly 64 bytes tr command below session.cookie.secret, authentication.cookie.secret, flash.cookie.secret exactly 64 bytes tr command below session.cookie.key, authentication.cookie.key, flash.cookie.key at least 64 bytes tr command below application.api.key at least 64 bytes tr command below application.admin.secret TOTP secret, Base32 tr -dc 'A-Z2-7' or TotpUtils.createSecret() application.admin.password Argon2id hash mvn -q mangooio:hash, see Administration persistence.mongo.password, smtp.password password of the service set in MongoDB or given by the SMTP provider

Use a separate random value for every key. The cookie secrets and keys fall back to application.secret, but dedicated values per cookie are recommended. Create the random values in one go:

mkdir -p secrets && cd secrets
umask 077
for key in application.secret \
           session.cookie.secret session.cookie.key \
           authentication.cookie.secret authentication.cookie.key \
           flash.cookie.secret flash.cookie.key; do
  LC_ALL=C tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 64 > "$key"
done
LC_ALL=C tr -dc 'A-Z2-7' < /dev/urandom | head -c 64 > application.admin.secret
printf '%s' 'the-mongo-password' > persistence.mongo.password

umask 077 makes the files readable by their owner only, wc -c < application.secret prints 64. A single trailing line break is removed when the file is read, more than one breaks the length check.

docs.title: compose.yaml
docs.text:
Mount the whole directory, a new secret is then just a new file:

services:
  myapp:
    image: myapp:latest
    user: "10001:10001"
    environment:
      JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS: "-Xms512m -Xmx1024m"
    volumes:
      - ./secrets:/run/secrets:ro

Without Swarm the secrets: block of Compose is a bind mount per file as well, so the directory mount offers the same protection with one line. Use the secrets: block with Docker Swarm, which stores secrets encrypted and mounts them on tmpfs. Use the long syntax there and set target to the config key, so the file name inside the container does not depend on which characters Swarm allows in secret names:

services:
  myapp:
    secrets:
      - source: application_secret
        target: application.secret
secrets:
  application_secret:
    external: true

Podman does the same with podman secret create and --secret <name>,target=<config key>.

docs.title: config.yaml
docs.text:
Set every key that comes from a file to file{} in the prod section:

environments:
  prod:
    application:
      secret: file{}
    session:
      cookie:
        secret: file{}
        key: file{}
    persistence:
      mongo:
        password: file{}

A key set to file{} without a file fails the startup and names the key. Use file{?} for a key that may be missing.

docs.title: File permissions
docs.text:
A bind mount keeps owner and permissions of the host, so the container user must be able to read the directory and its files. Give it a fixed numeric id, in the image with useradd --uid 10001 or with user: in compose.yaml, and hand directory and files to that id. Change the permissions first, after the chown your own user can no longer list the directory:

chmod 0400 secrets/*
chmod 0500 secrets
sudo chown -R 10001:10001 secrets

The application refuses to start as root in prod mode, so a permission problem can not be solved by running the container as root.

Without Compose, mount the directory the same way, docker run -v "$PWD/secrets:/run/secrets:ro" myapp, or point APPLICATION_SECRETS_PATH to another directory.

docs.title: Without Docker
docs.text:
file{} works the same without a container, the files and their names do not change. Outside a container /run is a tmpfs that is emptied on every reboot, so keep the files in a permanent directory and point APPLICATION_SECRETS_PATH to it:

sudo mkdir -p /etc/myapp/secrets

Create the files as described in Creating the secret files, then hand them to the user the application runs as. Change the permissions first, after the chown your own user can no longer list the directory:

sudo chmod 0400 /etc/myapp/secrets/*
sudo chmod 0500 /etc/myapp/secrets
sudo chown -R myapp:myapp /etc/myapp/secrets

systemd:

[Service]
User=myapp
Environment=APPLICATION_SECRETS_PATH=/etc/myapp/secrets
ExecStart=/usr/bin/java -Dapplication.mode=prod -jar /opt/myapp/myapp.jar

With LoadCredential= the files can stay readable by root only. systemd copies them on start into a directory of the service that only the service user can read, %d is that directory:

[Service]
User=myapp
LoadCredential=application.secret:/etc/myapp/secrets/application.secret
LoadCredential=persistence.mongo.password:/etc/myapp/secrets/persistence.mongo.password
Environment=APPLICATION_SECRETS_PATH=%d
ExecStart=/usr/bin/java -Dapplication.mode=prod -jar /opt/myapp/myapp.jar

For supervisord set APPLICATION_SECRETS_PATH in environment=, see Operating.

docs.title: External configuration
docs.text:
You can also point the whole configuration file elsewhere, which is useful when your deployment mounts config outside the JAR entirely (a Kubernetes ConfigMap or Secret, for instance) instead of baking it into the artifact:

java -Dapplication.config=/etc/myapp/config.yaml -jar myapp.jar

docs.title: HTTPS certificates
docs.text:
An HTTPS connector reads its key and certificate chain from a PKCS12 file:

connector:
  https:
    host: 0.0.0.0
    port: 8443
    keystore: /etc/myapp/https.p12
    password: file{}

connector.https.certificate.alias selects the entry and may stay empty if the file holds exactly one key entry. The connector accepts TLS 1.3 only; clients that need TLS 1.2 have to connect through a proxy that terminates TLS. Behind a load balancer TLS usually ends at the proxy and the application runs plain HTTP, see Operating. For local HTTPS a tool like mkcert creates a trusted certificate.

See Configuration for all keys and Migrations for the move from the vault of 10.x.

docs.title: Sessions 🍪
docs.text:
mangoo I/O stores session data in an encrypted and signed JWT cookie. Any instance that has the same cookie key, the same cookie secret, and the same application.name can read it. There is no server-side session store.

Browsers cap a cookie at about 4 KB. Store an id and a few flags, and keep the rest in the database. Cookie name, signing key, and SameSite are in Configuration. Lifetime is session.cookie.token.expires together with session.cookie.expires. There is no sliding expiry: a rewrite keeps the original exp.

Pass Session into the controller method:

package controllers;

import io.mangoo.routing.Response;
import io.mangoo.routing.bindings.Session;

public class SessionController {
    public Response session(Session session) {
        session.put("foo", "this is a session value");
        return Response.ok();
    }
}

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
session.put("key", "value");
session.get("key");
session.remove("key");
session.clear();       // empties values and expires the cookie
session.invalidate();  // expires the cookie, values stay readable
session.keep();        // persist a session that was created on this request
session.getCsrf();
session.hasContent();

A new cookie is written when put, remove, or clear changed the values, or when keep() was called on a session that was not restored from a cookie. keep() is what <@csrfform/> and <@csrftoken/> call so a freshly created CSRF token is actually stored. It does not refresh exp, and it does nothing useful for a session that was already restored.

clear() and invalidate() both send the cookie with Max-Age: 0. clear() replaces the value map. getCsrf() still returns the token for the rest of this request. invalidate() only marks the cookie for expiry.

The keys iss, aud, sub, iat, nbf, exp, jti and x-csrf-token are reserved, since the session is stored as claims inside the JWT; put() rejects them with an IllegalArgumentException.

docs.title: Cookie settings
docs.text:
session:
  cookie:
    name: myapp-session
    expires: false
    token:
      expires: 3600
    secure: true
    samesitemode: Strict
    secret: env{}
    key: env{}
  • session.cookie.expires: false (the default) keeps a browser-session cookie that disappears when the browser closes. true instead sets an actual expiry taken from session.cookie.token.expires, useful if you want a session to survive a browser restart.
  • session.cookie.token.expires: JWT lifetime in seconds (default 3600). Once this passes, the cookie decodes as expired regardless of what session.cookie.expires says about the cookie itself.
  • The cookie is always HttpOnly and Path=/. samesitemode must be Strict or Lax. Anything else fails startup. The default is Strict.
  • session.cookie.secret is exactly 64 bytes. session.cookie.key is at least 64 bytes. Both fall back to application.secret. JWT checks allow 30 seconds of clock skew. Set dedicated values with env{}, arg{}, or file{}. See Secrets.

See CSRF for how the session holds the CSRF token used to protect form submissions.

docs.title: Server-Sent Events
docs.text:
Server-Sent Events (SSE) let the server push updates to the browser over a long-lived HTTP connection. Unlike WebSockets, traffic is one-way (server → client) and uses ordinary HTTP, which plays well with proxies and load balancers that struggle with upgrade headers.

mangoo I/O maps SSE endpoints in routing and sends events from your own controller or service code. For bidirectional or binary protocols, reach for WebSockets instead, see the note in Routing.

docs.title: Routing
docs.text:
Bind.serverSentEvent().to("/sse");

SSE endpoints are not authenticated

SSE routes are registered directly on Undertow's path handler and therefore bypass the framework's handler chain entirely, including the authentication check that withAuthentication() provides for controller routes. There is no withAuthentication() on an SSE route, and none of the framework's access control applies to one.

Every SSE endpoint is reachable by anyone who knows the URL. The default handler groups connections by request URI, so send(path, data) reaches every client on that path. Do not push anything you would not serve from a public controller.

A custom connection handler can check a token, reject the connection, and key the ones it accepts per user. The framework still does not authenticate the route for you.

docs.title: Sending
docs.text:
import io.mangoo.manager.ServerSentEventManager;
import jakarta.inject.Inject;

public class NotifyService {
    private final ServerSentEventManager sse;

    @Inject
    public NotifyService(ServerSentEventManager sse) {
        this.sse = sse;
    }

    public void sendData() {
        sse.send("/sse", "{\"status\":\"ok\"}");
    }
}

The first argument is the key the connections are held under. For the default handler that is the request URI. The payload is a plain string.

Client writes run on virtual threads. With persistence enabled, send also inserts into mangooio_messages on the calling thread before it returns, so a slow MongoDB stalls the caller. Other instances tail that capped collection and skip documents they published themselves. There is no replay. An instance that is restarting, or a tail that is disconnected, misses those events. Without persistence the broker is in-memory and send reaches only the connections on this JVM.

removeConnection(key, connection) drops one connection. closeAll() closes every connection this instance holds. Shutdown does that before it drains in-flight controller requests.

docs.title: Custom connection handler
docs.text:
Everything above is what the default handler gives you: every connection of a route lands under the route URL, and send() is a broadcast to all of them. When you need to look at a connection before accepting it, or address a single client rather than a whole path, pass your own Undertow ServerSentEventConnectionCallback to the route:

Bind.serverSentEvent().to("/sse/client").withHandler(MyServerSentEventHandler.class);

withHandler is optional. A route without it behaves exactly as described above, so this changes nothing for endpoints you already have.

The handler is instantiated by Guice, so it can inject whatever it needs. It replaces the default handler completely, which means it owns everything the default one did:

  • Registering the connection, or deliberately not registering it. There is no automatic registration behind your back, so a connection your handler drops on the floor is simply never addressable.
  • Attaching a close task, so the connection is removed again when the client goes away. ServerSentEventCloseListener removes a connection by its request URI, so it stays usable as long as you register under connection.getRequestURI(). Under any other key, the close task has to call removeConnection(key, connection) itself.
public class MyServerSentEventHandler implements ServerSentEventConnectionCallback {
    @Override
    public void connected(ServerSentEventConnection connection, String lastEventId) {
        Deque<String> tokens = connection.getQueryParameters().get("token");
        String user = tokens == null ? null : authenticate(tokens.peekFirst());

        if (user == null) {
            connection.shutdown();
            return;
        }

        ServerSentEventManager manager = Application.getInstance(ServerSentEventManager.class);
        manager.addConnection(user, connection);
        connection.addCloseTask(closed -> manager.removeConnection(user, closed));
    }
}

The connection is now held under the user rather than under /sse/client, so send("someUser", data) reaches that one user and nobody else. Everything a key holds is still a list, so a user connected from two tabs receives the event on both.

connected() runs on an I/O thread, so keep it short and move anything blocking - a database lookup for the token, for example - onto a virtual thread, the way the default handler does.

docs.title: Proxies and load balancers
docs.text:
Every SSE route, including one with a custom handler, is prepared for running behind a reverse proxy such as nginx:

  • The response carries X-Accel-Buffering: no, so nginx passes each event on immediately instead of buffering it, and Cache-Control: no-cache.
  • A comment line is sent every 30 seconds while a connection is otherwise idle. Clients ignore comments, but the traffic keeps proxies and load balancers from closing the connection after their idle timeout.
  • The response headers are sent as soon as the connection is established, so the client's onopen fires right away. A handler does not need to send anything on connect.

What the application cannot set is the proxy's own connection handling. For nginx, use HTTP/1.1 towards the upstream and keep proxy_read_timeout above the 30 second heartbeat (the default of 60 seconds is fine):

location /sse {
    proxy_pass http://app;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;
    proxy_set_header Connection "";
}

On shutdown every SSE connection is closed before open requests are drained, as an open connection would otherwise hold the shutdown until its timeout. Browsers reconnect automatically and reach another instance through the load balancer.

Client setup: MDN Server-sent events.

docs.title: Templating 🖼️
docs.text:
Server-rendered HTML uses Freemarker. Templates are .ftl files under src/main/resources/templates/. Response.ok().render() resolves templates/<ControllerSimpleName>/<methodName>.ftl unless you pass template(...).

The engine uses HTML output format, so ${...} is escaped. Raw markup needs ?no_esc. ?api is enabled. The number format is 0.######. In dev mode templates are checked about once a second. A .ftl change does not restart mangooio:run. Outside dev mode the template cache does not expire.

Every render gets form, session, flash, i18n(...), route(...), location(...), prettytime(...), and the CSRF directives. Do not pass a model value with one of those names. The built-in replaces it.

See Controllers for how to pass model data with .render("key", value). For forms and CSRF, combine templating with Forms and CSRF.

docs.title: Built-in variables
docs.text:
These names are injected into every template automatically:

form
flash
session
i18n
route
location
prettytime

A model value with one of these names is replaced by the built-in. The failure usually shows up later in the template, not on the render call.

CSRF helpers (see CSRF):

<@csrfform/>
<@csrftoken/>

docs.title: Pretty time
docs.text:
Turns a date or timestamp into a relative description ("3 hours ago"), localized from the request locale rather than a fixed locale, so the same template reads naturally for users in different languages:

${prettytime(localDateTime)}
${prettytime(localDate)}
${prettytime(date)}

docs.title: Location
docs.text:
location(...) is true when the current request is mapped to that controller method. The match is case-insensitive. location("ApplicationController") with no method is true for every method on that controller:

<#if location("ApplicationController:index")>current</#if>

docs.title: Reverse routes
docs.text:
<a href="${route("ApplicationController:show")}">Show</a>
<a href="${route("ApplicationController:show", "42")}">Show 42</a>

If show is mapped to /users/{id}, the second example becomes /users/42. Pass one argument per placeholder. A missing argument fails the render. The key is simpleName:method, case-insensitive. Two controllers with the same simple name share one reverse route.

docs.title: Internationalization
docs.text:
${i18n("welcome")}
${i18n("hello", "Ada")}

See Internationalization for how message keys and locale resolution work.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Integration-style HTTP tests are supported through the mangooio-test artifact. It starts the real application stack in test mode, with the same routing, config merge, and handlers as production, and exposes helpers to send requests against the configured HTTP connector.

That approach catches issues unit tests miss entirely: wrong routes, filter ordering, cookie handling, and template rendering. The trade-off is speed, since the app is booted once via TestRunner and shared by all test classes of the JVM, so keep individual tests focused and do not rely on state another test class left behind.

Add the dependency to your pom.xml:

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.mangoo</groupId>
    <artifactId>mangooio-test</artifactId>
    <version>11.0.0</version>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>

Use the latest published version rather than the placeholder shown above.

docs.title: Starting the application
docs.text:
Extend your tests with io.mangoo.test.TestRunner, and it starts mangoo I/O in test mode once per JVM; all test classes share that instance:

import io.mangoo.test.TestRunner;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.ExtendWith;

@ExtendWith(TestRunner.class)
class ApplicationControllerTest {
}

Override beforeStartup() / afterStartup() if you need to set system properties before Application.start(Mode.TEST) runs. The application starts once per JVM. Only the extension instance that wins that start runs the hooks, so a subclass used as @ExtendWith is what makes an override reliable. -Dapplication.mode still wins over Mode.TEST. close() does nothing. The runner does not shut the JVM down.

docs.title: HTTP requests
docs.text:
import io.mangoo.test.http.TestRequest;
import io.mangoo.test.http.TestResponse;
import io.undertow.util.StatusCodes;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import static org.hamcrest.MatcherAssert.assertThat;
import static org.hamcrest.Matchers.*;

@Test
void testIndex() {
    TestResponse response = TestRequest.get("/").execute();

    assertThat(response, not(nullValue()));
    assertThat(response.getStatusCode(), equalTo(StatusCodes.OK));
    assertThat(response.getContent(), containsString("Hello"));
}

Factory methods cover every verb you would need: TestRequest.get/post/put/patch/delete/head/options(uri).

Chain on fluent extras before calling execute():

TestRequest.post("/save")
    .withHeader("X-Request-Id", "1")
    .withContentType("application/json")
    .withStringBody("{\"name\":\"Ada\"}")
    .withCookie(cookie)
    .withBasicAuthentication("user", "pass")
    .withDisabledRedirects()
    .withTimeout(5, ChronoUnit.SECONDS)
    .execute();

withForm(Multimap) forces POST and sends application/x-www-form-urlencoded.

execute() always calls http://{connector.http.host}:{connector.http.port}. An HTTPS-only application is not what this client talks to. Redirects are followed unless withDisabledRedirects() is set. The request timeout defaults to 5 seconds, and the connect timeout is 5 seconds. withBasicAuthentication installs a JDK Authenticator. It does not set an Authorization header itself.

There is no helper for WebSocket or SSE connections. See Routing.

docs.title: Browser sessions
docs.text:
TestBrowser keeps cookies across calls, so it can carry a login through to later requests:

import io.mangoo.test.http.TestBrowser;
import io.undertow.util.Methods;
import io.undertow.util.StatusCodes;

TestBrowser browser = TestBrowser.open();

TestResponse login = browser.to("/dologin")
    .withHTTPMethod(Methods.POST.toString())
    .withDisabledRedirects()
    .execute();

assertThat(login.getStatusCode(), equalTo(StatusCodes.FOUND));

TestResponse account = browser.to("/authenticationrequired")
    .withHTTPMethod(Methods.GET.toString())
    .execute();

docs.title: Email and concurrency
docs.text:
io.mangoo.test.email.SmtpMock binds GreenMail to smtp.host and smtp.port. start() does nothing outside dev and test, and it does not change smtp.protocol. GreenMail speaks plain SMTP, so set smtp.protocol: smtp and an unprivileged port such as 3025 in the test environment. Obtain the mock with Application.getInstance(SmtpMock.class). Call start() / stop() around the test and read captured messages from getGreenMail().

io.mangoo.test.concurrent.ConcurrentRunner runs a Cactoos Func on many virtual threads. The default count is availableProcessors() << 4. It is a Hamcrest matcher, not a java.util.function type.

io.mangoo.test.hamcrest.RegexMatcher.matches(regex) lets you assert on response bodies with a regular expression instead of an exact string match.

docs.title: Utils
docs.text:
The framework exposes small, focused helper classes in io.mangoo.utils. Prefer these over reimplementing crypto, JWT, or file logic yourself in application code. Types under io.mangoo.utils.internal are not public API and may change without notice, so avoid depending on them directly.

Common tasks covered: Argon2 password hashing (CommonUtils), JWT creation and parsing (JwtUtils), TOTP for admin MFA (TotpUtils), JSON helpers (JsonUtils), and file/stream utilities (FileUtils).

docs.title: CommonUtils
docs.text:
Argon2id hashing, encoding, UUIDs, and small helpers:

String hash = CommonUtils.hashArgon2("password", "salt");
boolean ok = CommonUtils.matchArgon2("password", "salt", hash);

String id = CommonUtils.uuidV7();   // also uuidV4(), uuidV6()
String random = CommonUtils.randomString(32);

byte[] encoded = CommonUtils.encodeToBase64("payload");
byte[] decoded = CommonUtils.decodeFromBase64(new String(encoded, StandardCharsets.UTF_8));

hashArgon2(cleartext) uses application.secret as salt and embeds it in the stored hash. Use the two-argument form with a random salt per user. Both need a started application. hashArgon2(cleartext, salt, settings) hashes with the given Argon2Settings and does not. mvn mangooio:hash uses that form. Both hashArgon2 and matchArgon2 throw an unchecked MangooHashingException when no hashing slot becomes free within authentication.hashing.timeout. matchArgon2 does not report that as a mismatch. See Argon2 hashing.

hexSHA512 is SHA3-512 and returns null on failure. randomString(int) requires a length from 22 to 512 and uses URL-safe Base64. serializeToBase64 and deserializeFromBase64 need registerSerializable(Class) first, and only for data you trust. bitLength checks key material.

docs.title: JwtUtils
docs.text:
Sessions, authentication, and the admin cookie all use Nimbus JOSE+JWT (HS512 + JWE) under the hood. You can also issue tokens yourself for your own use cases:

withKey and withSecret take byte[]. createJwt and parseJwt throw the checked MangooJwtException. The key is HMAC-SHA-512 and must be at least 64 bytes. The secret is the direct A256CBC-HS512 key and must be exactly 64 bytes. JwtUtils does not check those lengths itself. Nimbus fails later. Clock skew is fixed at 30 seconds, and nbf is set to now minus 30 seconds. Reserved claim names are rejected. withClaims(Map<String, String>) and withJwtID(String) add claims. extractCustomClaims(JWTClaimsSet) reads the ones that are not reserved.

byte[] signingKey = ...;       // at least 64 bytes
byte[] encryptionSecret = ...; // exactly 64 bytes

var data = JwtUtils.JwtData.create()
    .withKey(signingKey)
    .withSecret(encryptionSecret)
    .withIssuer("myapp")
    .withAudience("myapp-api")
    .withSubject("user-1")
    .withTtlSeconds(3600);

String jwt = JwtUtils.createJwt(data);
JWTClaimsSet claims = JwtUtils.parseJwt(jwt, data);

Pull the key material from env{} or file{}. See Secrets.

docs.title: TotpUtils
docs.text:
SHA-512 TOTP with 6 digits and a 30-second period, matching what the admin dashboard uses. See Authentication.

String secret = TotpUtils.createSecret();
boolean valid = TotpUtils.verifyTotp(secret, code);
String qr = TotpUtils.getQRCode("user@example.com", "My App", secret);

verifyTotp(secret, code) accepts a valid code any number of times. verifyTotp(identifier, secret, code) accepts each step once and keeps it until (counter + 2) * 30 seconds. createSecret() is 64 Base32 characters. getQRCode returns a Base64 PNG, not a data URI. getTotp(secret) returns the current code. There is no adjacent-step window. Only the current 30-second step matches.

docs.title: DateUtils
docs.text:
Date date = DateUtils.localDateTimeToDate(LocalDateTime.now()); // application.timezone
Date day = DateUtils.localDateToDate(LocalDate.now());
String relative = DateUtils.getPrettyTime(LocalDateTime.now()); // fixed locale en-EN
String de = DateUtils.getPrettyTime(Locale.GERMAN, LocalDateTime.now());

docs.title: JsonUtils
docs.text: See Working with JSON: toJson, toPrettyJson, toObject, toFlatMap, getMapper().

docs.title: FileUtils
docs.text:
String mime = FileUtils.getMimeType(bytes);
String size = FileUtils.readableFileSize(2048);
String text = FileUtils.readFileToString(path);
FileUtils.closeQuietly(stream);

docs.title: RequestUtils
docs.text:
Optional<String> bearer = RequestUtils.getAuthorizationHeader(request);
Map<String, String> params = RequestUtils.getRequestParameters(exchange);

docs.title: PersistenceUtils
docs.text: Maps @Collection classes to MongoDB collection names. You will rarely call this yourself, since the framework already registers collections at startup.

docs.title: Argument
docs.text: Argument.requireNonBlank(value, "value");

docs.title: Crypto
docs.text: io.mangoo.crypto.Crypto encrypts strings with AES-256-GCM. The key is SHA-256 of the secret after non-ASCII characters are stripped, and at least 32 characters have to remain. encrypt(String, String) and decrypt(String, String) return null on failure. They do not throw. RSA is 3072-bit RSA/None/OAEPWITHSHA-512ANDMGF1PADDING and throws the checked MangooEncryptionException. generateKeyPair(), getKeyAsString(Key), getPrivateKeyFromString (PKCS#8 Base64), and getPublicKeyFromString (X.509 Base64) are the key helpers.

docs.title: Working with JSON 📦
docs.text:
REST and AJAX endpoints often need to return JSON instead of HTML. mangoo I/O uses Jackson with the Blackbird module for fast serialization, chosen specifically because Blackbird generates property accessors at startup instead of relying on reflection on every request, which matters once an endpoint is handling real traffic. Controller methods return Response.ok().bodyJson(...), or bind the request body to a type by declaring it as a parameter.

PATCH bodies are bound like POST and PUT: into a new instance, not merged into an existing object. Invalid JSON binds an empty instance created by the no-arg constructor (422 Unprocessable Content only if there is none). Failed Bean Validation yields 400, as an HTML page or, with passthrough mode, as JSON (see Controllers). For error payloads shaped consistently for API clients, bodyJsonError(...) returns the same structure every time, so a frontend does not need a special case for each endpoint's error format.

By default, null properties are omitted from output, which keeps payloads smaller and avoids leaking fields a client did not ask about. Use @JsonInclude to force a value out anyway (useful when a client genuinely needs to distinguish "explicitly null" from "field absent"), and @JsonIgnore to hide a field entirely, such as an internal comment that should never leave the server:

import com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation.JsonIgnore;
import com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation.JsonInclude;

public class Car {
    @JsonInclude
    public String brand = null;

    @JsonInclude
    public int doors = 0;

    @JsonIgnore
    public String comment = "internal";

    public String foo = "visible";
}

docs.title: JSON input
docs.text:
Automatic POJO binding works for POST, PUT, and PATCH requests sent with Content-Type: application/json:

package controllers;

import io.mangoo.routing.Response;
import models.Car;

public class JsonController {
    public Response parse(Car car) {
        return Response.ok().bodyJson(car);
    }
}

If deserialization fails, the parameter is a new instance created by the no-arg constructor; only if the class has none does it become UnprocessableContent and the framework returns HTTP 422, the same way a failed path or query parameter conversion does.

If you would rather not commit to a POJO, for example when the payload shape genuinely varies:

public Response parse(Request request) {
    Map<String, Object> json = request.getBodyAsJsonMap();
    String firstname = (String) json.get("firstname");
    return Response.ok();
}

getBodyAsJsonMap() returns an empty map for an empty body and null for invalid JSON.

Or work with the raw body directly, useful when you need to verify a signature over the exact bytes before touching the content:

public Response parse(Request request) {
    String body = request.getBody();
    return Response.ok();
}

JsonUtils offers the same conversions outside of request handling, for example inside a service class or a scheduled job:

import tools.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;

String json = JsonUtils.toJson(person);
String pretty = JsonUtils.toPrettyJson(person);
Person object = JsonUtils.toObject(json, Person.class);
Map<String, String> flat = JsonUtils.toFlatMap(json);
ObjectMapper mapper = JsonUtils.getMapper();

getMapper() returns Jackson 3's tools.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper. @JsonIgnore, @JsonInclude, @JsonProperty and @JsonCreator stay in com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation. java.util.Date is formatted in application.timezone. LocalDate and LocalDateTime carry no zone.

toJson() and toPrettyJson() return an empty string and toObject() returns null if conversion fails rather than throwing, and do not log the underlying exception. That is a deliberate trade-off: it keeps a single malformed object from crashing an otherwise unrelated code path, but it also means you should check the return value yourself if a null here would be a real problem for you, rather than assuming a non-null object always comes back.

docs.title: JSON output
docs.text:
Person person = new Person("Peter", "Parker", 24);
return Response.ok().bodyJson(person);

The body on the wire is compact, from JsonUtils.toJson. Null properties are omitted. The object above is the data, not the bytes. toPrettyJson is the pretty printer. A failed toJson inside bodyJson sends an empty body and the status you set.

Response.badRequest().bodyJsonError("Invalid payload") sends io.mangoo.models.Error: a timestamp without a zone, status, and message.
